activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons, so averaging a full year of bills gives a truer monthly cost than a single month's bill.
story:
Wyatt spread the two leases on his knees at the bus stop, holding the corners down when the wind lifted them. The one for the Marlowe building showed rent of six-fifty a month with heat included, all of it in tidy print. The one for the place on Fuller Street showed five-ninety, with a separate line for utilities paid by the tenant. He had been sure, on the walk over, that Fuller was the cheaper option by sixty dollars.

Leena sat down beside him with her bag on her lap. "Still doing that?"

"Still doing that." He turned to the back page of the Fuller lease, where the landlord had stapled a copy of last month's utility bill. August, it said across the top. Thirty-eight dollars.

"That's nothing," Leena said, peering over. "You could add forty to anything."

"I did add forty. It's still cheaper." He wrote the sum in the margin: six hundred and twenty-eight. He was about to fold the papers away when Juan arrived, earbuds around his neck, and dropped onto the bench on Wyatt's other side.

"Juan, look at this. Fuller's cheaper, right? Five-ninety plus the power bill."

Juan picked up the August bill and turned it over. "My abuela would tell you you're about to get robbed."

"What?"

"She had this thing about winter. When I wanted to move out last year she sat me down and said a summer bill tells you nothing, that heating and cooling change with the seasons, and you have to average a whole year of bills to know what a month really costs. She was recovering from her surgery then, convalescing at our place for a month, and she had nothing to do but lecture me about it. Twice a day." He handed the bill back. "Look at the date, man."

Wyatt looked at the date. August. He tried to remember the shape of his grandmother's own furnace, the way it clanked through January, but he had never once seen a bill for it. "I don't have a year of bills. I have one month."

Mr. Rahman came down the sidewalk with his grocery bag and stopped at the shelter to wait for the crosstown, as he did most afternoons. He nodded at the papers. "First apartment?"

"Two of them," Wyatt said. "One's got heat included in the rent. One doesn't, and the landlord only gave me this." He held up the August bill. "It's low."

"August would be," Mr. Rahman said. He did not go on. He took out his phone and checked the time.

Wyatt sat with the two numbers, six-fifty flat against five-ninety plus something unknown, and felt the decision tilt under him. The Marlowe number was boring and fixed. The Fuller number was a bet against January. "So I can't actually compare them," he said. "Not with what I've got. Unless the landlord sends the last year of bills."

"So ask him," Leena said.

"If he doesn't have them?"

"Then you're guessing." She said it without apology, the way she said most things, and Juan laughed and called her an ebullient little prosecutor, which she accepted as a compliment, because she meant it as her job description in miniature.

Wyatt took out his phone and photographed both leases, both totals, and typed an email to the Fuller landlord while the three of them watched the traffic. He wrote that he was interested but would need twelve months of utility history to compare the true monthly cost against the other unit. He read the sentence twice, deleted "true" and put it back, and sent it. The bus appeared at the far corner, still two lights away.

"There's a version of this where the landlord says the bills are private," Juan said, "and you still have to pick."

"I know." Wyatt folded the papers and squared them against his thigh. "But if he won't show me a year of them, that tells me something too." He wasn't sure what it told him exactly, whether a landlord guarding the winter bills was hiding a cost or just disorganized, and he said so.

Mr. Rahman's bus came first. He shouldered his grocery bag, then paused. "My nephew manages buildings. He says the good tenants are the ones who ask for the year." He stepped on, and the doors closed behind him.

The crosstown pulled in a minute later, brakes sighing. Leena stood, and Juan stood, and Wyatt stayed seated on the bench with the folded leases in his hand, watching his phone, which had not yet buzzed.

"I'll wait for the next one," he said. "I want to see if he answers."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with.
story:
The museum had exactly one exhibit on the French Revolution, wedged between a room of medieval coins and a café that smelled of soup. Tyson stood in front of the display case with his notebook open and nothing written in it. The essay was due in nine days, and Ms. Ramos had assigned the topic as though it were simple: how views of the Revolution had changed since 1800. Two thousand words on the arguments of historians he had never read, and so far his research consisted of one library book, three dead browser tabs, and this glass case containing a shoe buckle allegedly worn at the storming of the Bastille.

Tessa found him there twenty minutes later, carrying two lemonades from the café, one of which she handed over without comment. She was doing the same essay, which was either convenient or a problem.

"Is that the shoe buckle?" she said. "I read the placard. It says 'allegedly.'"

"Allegedly is doing a lot of work on that placard," Tyson said. He copied the word provenance off a small card in the case, which explained that the buckle's chain of ownership had been traced back only to 1850, after which the museum had simply stopped asking questions. It was, he thought, a nice example of how a story got sharper the less you looked at it.

They sat down on the bench across from the case, and he showed her his real problem. His library book was a collection of essays by twentieth-century historians, all of whom kept referring back to something called Reflections on the Revolution in France, by Edmund Burke, as though everyone in the world had read it. Tyson had not read it. He had read enough to know that Burke's book had come out in 1790, which was not merely before all the historians he was supposed to write about but before the century his essay was supposed to start from.

"So I can't use it," he said. "The essay starts at 1800."

"Can't or shouldn't?"

"Can't. The assignment says how views changed since 1800. This book is from 1790. It's before everything."

Tessa drank her lemonade and looked at the shoe buckle, which was small and grey and, allegedly, historic. "But every historian after 1800 is arguing with it. Isn't that what the book in your hand keeps saying?"

He had been treating this as an obstacle, a wall between the material he was allowed to use and the material that clearly mattered. He turned it over while a tour group shuffled past the coins. If the historians he was supposed to write about had spent two centuries positioning themselves against Burke, then Burke wasn't outside the essay. He was the ground it stood on. The trick would be to bring him in sideways: establish the position first, then show the seismic shifts away from it, one historian at a time. He started writing in the margin of his notebook: begin with what Burke condemned, not with when he published.

"Burke," Tessa said, reading over his shoulder, because she had no sense of boundaries. "This says he condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition. That's your opening line right there. He hated it because it tore things down."

"It's the conservative view," Tyson said. "Apparently everyone who wrote after 1800 had to argue with him or with somebody arguing with him." He wrote that down too, and underlined it, which was a habit Ms. Ramos had told him to break.

They spent another hour in the museum's small reading corner, where the Wi-Fi worked if you sat near the radiator. Tyson found a scanned excerpt of the Reflections and skimmed enough of Burke's prose to understand that the man would have hated the shoe buckle, the placard, and probably the lemonade. Tessa, meanwhile, drafted an outline that started in 1800 and never mentioned Burke at all, and when Tyson pointed out the problem with this, she said, "I'm leaving him in the second paragraph, where he belongs," in the tone of someone who had already decided the second paragraph was further away than the first.

By closing time he had a thesis, more or less: that the historians after 1800 had spent enormous energy either pulling away from Burke or dragging him back, and that his own essay could be honest about which side he found more convincing without pretending the question was settled. That was the part Ms. Ramos kept asking for, a considered position, and he suspected his considered position was that he trusted the pullers further than the draggers, except when he didn't. He could flag that uncertainty rather than preempt it with a tidy conclusion, which felt like a risk and also like the truth.

Outside, the October light was going flat and grey over the museum steps. Tessa zipped her bag and said, "Second paragraph, Tyson. I'm telling you."

"Third," he said, and held the door.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
story:
The county archive occupied the second floor of the library, above the children's room, and Katherine had never gone up before Tuesday. Mr. Martínez, who ran it, made her sign a ledger with a fountain pen that left a small blot beside her name. She had come for Marco Polo. Her world history paper was due in eleven days, and she had already written three paragraphs about the Silk Road that she suspected were mostly decorative.

"Primary sources only for the core argument," Mr. Martínez said, sliding a facsimile edition across the reading table. "The rest is garnish."

The facsimile was beautiful and useless to her. It reproduced a manuscript of the Travels in a hand she couldn't read, with marginal notes in something that might have been Latin or might have been shorthand for the monk who copied it. She spent an hour with it anyway, because handling a thing four hundred years old made the paper feel less like homework. Then she went to the shelf behind her and pulled down the secondary sources, the modern books, and one of them had a title that stopped her: something about whether Marco Polo had gone to China at all.

She read the author's name twice. Frances Wood. A historian, a real one, with a university listed on the jacket. Katherine sat down on the carpet between the stacks, which was against the rules, and read the argument whole.

At lunch the next day she found Jersey and Zion at the far table, the one by the recycling bin that everyone pretended not to want.

"My guy might be a fraud," Katherine said.

"Who," said Zion, not looking up from his phone.

"Marco Polo. There's a historian, Frances Wood, who argued he may never have reached China at all." She waited until Zion put the phone down. "His book never mentions tea. Never mentions foot-binding, or the Great Wall. Seventeen years, supposedly, and no tea."

Jersey frowned. "Maybe he didn't drink tea."

"Nobody in China didn't mention tea. It would be like going to America for seventeen years and never writing down anything about coffee. Or the flag." She was aware she was talking too fast. "Wood's point is about the silences. What's not in the book."

"So write about the journey," Zion said. "That was your topic."

"That was my topic before I knew the journey might not have happened."

"Then it's a better topic now," Jersey said, and stole one of Katherine's fries, which was how Jersey signaled that a conversation was worth having.

But it wasn't that simple, and Katherine knew it, and it sat badly with her all through sixth period. She had compartmentalized neatly until now: the report was one drawer, what she actually believed was another, and the two needn't speak. She had done it for the chemistry test she didn't care about, for the college essay about service that she'd embellished within an inch of its life. Something about the archive made the drawers stick. The manuscript she'd touched had been copied by a person who believed Polo, or was paid to copy him, and she couldn't put that person in a drawer.

She went back Thursday after last bell. Mr. Martínez was rehousing photographs in grey boxes, cotton gloves on, and he raised an eyebrow at her before she spoke.

"Do you decide who's right?" she asked. "When historians disagree. Is there an answer at the bottom?"

"Sometimes. Mostly not." He set down a photograph of a demolished mill. "Mostly you get a stack of partial sources and a question, and the question isn't fixed. People asked different things in 1900 than they ask now. What's your disagreement?"

"Whether Marco Polo went to China. Frances Wood says maybe he never did. No tea, no foot-binding, no Great Wall in the whole book."

"Wood's the British one, yes. There are others on the other side, defenders, if you look. They say plenty of things in the book that only someone who'd been there would know." He peeled off one glove. "What do you notice about that, about the two camps?"

She thought of the marginal notes on the facsimile, the monk's shorthand she couldn't read. "That they're both reading the same book."

"Go on."

"That they're asking it different questions." She heard herself say it and felt the floor tilt slightly, in a good way. "The ones who defend him are asking, is the detail accurate. The ones who doubt him are asking, what's missing. Same pages, different question."

Mr. Martínez smiled with half his mouth, which she was learning was his highest available praise. "That's not a resolution, mind you."

"I know."

She stayed until closing. She photocopied the pages where Wood laid out the omissions, then found a defender's book two shelves over and photocopied the pages where he called the omission argument, in a phrase she underlined twice, a pithy kind of misdirection, clever but thin. She could see the temptation of that word, the way it let him dismiss rather than answer. She wrote in her notebook, careful not to editorialize: both accounts rely on the same incomplete text. Neither can be checked against anything Polo himself wrote, because he dictated it all to a romance writer in a Genoese prison.

At home her mother asked how the paper was coming and Katherine said fine, which was true in a way, though the paper now had a hole in its middle where the journey used to be and she had not decided what to put there. She drafted two openings that night. One began, Marco Polo's account has shaped the world's image of China for centuries. The other began, The most famous travel book ever written may describe a journey its author never took.

She read them both aloud to her bedroom, quietly, and left both on the screen. Then she pulled the photocopies from her bag, squared the edges, and set the missing one, the tea, the foot-binding, the Wall, on top of the stack.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
story:
The kettle on his grandfather's stove had a loose handle, and you had to hold it with a folded tea towel or risk a burn. Nicolas held it now, watching the water go cloudy at the bottom before it cleared and then, all at once, began to roll. His textbook lay open on the counter beside a plate of shortbread, and his notebook was propped against the toaster, which was the only place in the kitchen where the light was any good.

"So you're telling me," his grandfather said, settling into the chair by the window, "that heat makes everything go faster, and yet the reaction goes backward. That's like saying a pay rise makes you poorer."

Nicolas had come to the house for the quiet, mostly. His mother had suggested it when the apartment got loud with his little cousins, and his grandfather had said only, "Bring the biscuit tin back full," which Nicolas had forgotten to do. But it turned out the old man read over his shoulder, which was worse than noise.

"It's not backward exactly," Nicolas said. "It's shifted. There's a forward reaction and a reverse one, happening at the same time, and equilibrium is when they balance out."

"Equilibrium," his grandfather repeated, in the tone he used for words like stagflation, which he had been lambasting all winter in the margins of his newspaper, drawing arrows between articles that confirmed his view of the economy. "Everything balances until something comes along and knocks it sideways. Then it finds a new balance. I've seen it in my own savings. Fine, fine. Go on."

Nicolas copied the equilibrium arrow into his notes, the two half-heads facing opposite directions, and stared at the example about heating a mixture. The trouble was simple and it wouldn't leave him alone. Raising the temperature speeds things up. If heat speeds up the forward reaction, the mixture should make more product, forward, forward, forward. But the book said the equilibrium shifted the other way, toward the reverse, when you heated this one. He had underlined the sentence twice and understood it zero times.

Viviane, over the phone, was no help at first. "Just memorize it," she said. "Hot shifts it one way, cold shifts the other, that's the whole trick. Kiana made flashcards, you could copy hers."

"That's not knowing it, that's wearing it," Nicolas said, and then apologised, because he knew how he sounded. Through the phone he could hear her sister practising the same four bars of piano again and again, never getting past a missed note.

He put the kettle back on because his grandfather wanted a second cup, and while he waited he read the paragraph a third time, slowly, the way Mr. Campbell-Brown had told them to read anything that contradicted their intuition. There it was, one sentence he'd skimmed: raising the temperature speeds up both directions. Both. And then the comparison he'd missed entirely, tucked in a subordinate clause as if it were nothing: it speeds up the endothermic direction more. He sat back. It wasn't that heat pushed everything forward and everything got faster together. Both sides got faster, but not equally, and the one that absorbed heat got the bigger push, the way the loose-handled kettle took the water from calm to rolling all at once rather than degree by degree. That was why the equilibrium shifted toward the endothermic side when you heated it. Not a push. A difference between two pushes.

"So?" his grandfather said. "You've stopped sighing."

"Both directions speed up," Nicolas said, mostly to the kettle. "But the endothermic one speeds up more. That's the whole thing. That's why the shift happens."

"Sounds like the economy again," his grandfather said, phlegmatic about it, as he was phlegmatic about most disasters that arrived slowly. "Everything grows, some things grow faster, and the balance point moves whether you like it or not. Nobody votes on the new balance." He took his tea and drank it and said nothing further, which Nicolas was learning was the man's way of approving.

He called Viviane back. "Okay, don't memorize it. Heat speeds up the forward reaction and the reverse reaction, both, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more. That's why heating shifts the equilibrium that way."

There was a silence on the line, then the piano stopped mid-bar. "Say that again," Viviane said. "Slower. Kiana, put the flashcards away, he's got something."

He said it again, and it held together both times, which was the only test he trusted. What he still couldn't answer, and said so, was why heat chose to speed the endothermic side more, what was happening down there at the level he couldn't see, and Viviane said, "Maybe next year," and hung up on her sister's behalf.

The kitchen had gone dark without his noticing. His grandfather was asleep in the chair, teacup balanced on his knee, and the newspaper on his lap had fallen open to the letters page, its margins crowded with his arrows, every equilibrium he knew knocked sideways and finding its level anyway. Nicolas took the cup quietly, set it in the sink, and rinsed it under the cold tap until the steam stopped rising.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
James had never once lost his composure at a tournament, which was why Mr. Nakamura had trusted him with the one-act in the first place. That was how James told it, anyway, and he told it twice on the bus: once to Romain, who was highlightering his affirmative case, and once to Elijah, who was asleep against the window and therefore, by James's accounting, an ideal listener. The one-act was going to be fine. He had the whole second scene blocked in his head, every entrance and cross, and the fact that he had never actually stood the actors on their feet to try any of it was, he explained, a scheduling matter, not an artistic one.

The tournament was held in a high school that smelled of floor wax and vending machines. James's round wasn't until after lunch, so between rounds he found an empty classroom, pushed the desks against the wall, and laid a rectangle of tape on the floor where the stage would be. Romain came in carrying two milks from the cafeteria and said the rectangle was crooked. James said it was intentional, a forced perspective. Romain looked at the tape, then at James, and drank one of the milks.

Elijah arrived a few minutes later, still in his tie, still half-asleep, and agreed to read the other part. James stood where the audience would be, which was the back of a chair by the chalkboard, and watched his own scene with what he considered a director's eye. Elijah played Michael, the brother who stays. James had written the scene so that Michael and Daniel argue about the father's house, and Michael has the longer speeches, the ones with the real weight. Elijah delivered them facing the tape rectangle's upstage edge, which is to say, facing away from the chair entirely.

"Turn," James said, and Elijah turned, and James lost the argument.

It wasn't Elijah's fault, and James knew it wasn't, because James had blocked it that way. He had drawn the scene on graph paper, arrows and X's, and the arrows looked right, the geometry was clean, and the geometry was wrong. From the chair, Michael's argument about the house was a back. A whole page of dialogue delivered to the cinderblock wall. Romain, from his seat on a desk, said the wall probably disagreed with Daniel anyway. James told him to be quiet, and later he would remember having said it kindly.

What he did next, he would later describe as instinct, though at the time it felt more like panic moving slowly. He stepped onto the tape rectangle and took Elijah's place, facing the same wrong direction, and asked Romain to read Daniel from where Elijah had stood. He said his own lines at the wall, and his voice went flat into the cinderblock, and he could feel the words not carrying, dying somewhere around the third row of a real theatre he was only imagining. Then, without deciding to, he angled his shoulders, kept his eyes on Romain, and let his body open toward the chair. The line landed. He did it again with the next speech. His face, half-turned, half-visible, carried the sentence to the back of the room the way it hadn't before.

"Cheating out," Elijah said from the desk, waking up properly for the first time all day. "It's called cheating out. We did it in middle school."

"You did theatre in middle school and you let me figure that out on a chair?" James said, but he was already re-marking the blocking in his notebook, drawing the diagonal. He wrote the words down too, because he suspected he would need them again, and because he had an incipient suspicion that his graph paper had other errors of the same species, errors that looked correct from above and wrong from the front.

He ran the scene four more times, and each time he found something the paper hadn't shown him. When both actors cheated out in the final exchange, they formed a slight V, and the V did something to the argument that James couldn't name yet, made it seem less like two positions and more like two people who had once shared a kitchen. He thought about his own debate rounds, the way he'd been taught to interpolate the opponent's evidence into his rebuttal, taking their sentences and rehousing them in his argument, and he thought the stage wanted something almost opposite: you kept your body angled toward the room even while you addressed the other person, so the audience got both faces at once. He wasn't sure the two crafts had anything real in common. He suspected it was a nice thought, the kind you have instead of a conclusion.

Romain, who had to prep for octofinals, left with the second milk unfinished. Elijah stayed for one more run and then checked his phone and said the pairings were up. James gathered the tape slowly, peeling it off in long strips, because his own round was also coming and he hadn't looked at his flows since morning, which he would later describe as a controlled decision. In the hallway, Mr. Nakamura was posting schematics on the corkboard and asked, without looking up, how the directing was going. James said the blocking was basically locked. He believed this, mostly, the way he believed he had never once lost his composure, though his hands were still humming from the tape and he kept turning the notebook over, checking that the words were still there.

"Basically locked," Mr. Nakamura repeated, in a tone James chose to hear as approval. He went to find his round room, walking a little open-shouldered, angled toward the corridor as if it were full of chairs.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
The planetarium smelled of dust and projection oil, and Brayden had claimed the back row of the dome as his study spot because nobody bothered him there between school shows. Ms. Sánchez let him stay after closing if he kept the lights low and locked up himself. He spread his notes across three seats: a printout of the Keeling curve, a chapter on radiative forcing, and a practice question that had beaten him twice already.

"How do greenhouse gases trap heat," Eugenie read over his shoulder, having arrived uninvited with Christine and a bag of gas station candy. "That's the whole quiz, isn't it."

"That's the whole quiz," Brayden said. He tapped the graph, the line climbing in its jagged sawtooth, up and up across the decades. "This part I can read. Carbon dioxide, parts per million, measured every year since before my grandmother was born. It goes up. But the question wants the mechanism, and I keep writing myself into a corner."

Christine dropped into the seat beside him and unwrapped a peanut butter cup with surgical care. "So write it. Common gases trap heat. Done."

"That's what I wrote," Brayden said. "Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, so they must be doing most of the trapping. More of something, more effect. That's just arithmetic."

Eugenie shook her head slowly, and Christine was already digging in her backpack, saying, "You did the reading wrong," which stung more than if she'd called him stupid. She found the textbook, its spine cracked at the climate chapter, and turned it toward him without a word.

He read it twice. Nitrogen and oxygen made up about ninety-nine percent of dry air, and neither was a greenhouse gas, because molecules made of two identical atoms did not absorb infrared radiation. He sat back. The dome ceiling above him was scattered with projected stars left over from the last show, torpid and slightly out of focus, wheeling above seats that held nobody. He had been so certain of his arithmetic that he'd never thought to check what the molecules were doing, only how many of them there were.

"So the entire trapping job falls on the trace stuff," he said. "The point-one percent. Carbon dioxide, water vapor. The graph isn't rising because the air is getting bigger. It's rising because the rare gases are getting less rare." He looked at the sawtooth line again and it was a different graph now, the way a word looks different once you learn it. "I want to say the atmosphere is like a club where almost nobody at the door can get in, and then suddenly a million more of the right people show up."

"That's the worst sentence I've ever heard," Eugenie said, but she was smiling.

"I'd put it on a slide, though," Christine said. "Kids remember worst sentences." She pointed at the small print under the graph, where the data source was named, an observatory on a volcano in the middle of the Pacific. "Why measure it on a volcano? Why not somewhere normal?"

"Somewhere normal has a power plant down the road and a highway upwind," Brayden said. "You'd be measuring the parking lot, not the planet." He wrote volcano, clean air, baseline in the margin. His grandfather, convalescing after his surgery and hooked on documentaries, had put it a different way over Thanksgiving: you don't take a town's temperature in the boiler room. Brayden had thought it was just an old man being colorful. Now it sounded like experimental design.

Ms. Sánchez came through with her keys jangling and stopped at the edge of their row. "You three are the reason the utility bill thinks we run night shows." She nodded at his notes. "Explain it to me like I'm eight. I'll tell you if you pass."

Brayden stood under the false stars. "Almost all the air is nitrogen and oxygen, and they can't absorb the infrared the Earth radiates out at night, because they're two identical atoms each. So heat that would escape just passes them by. The gases that do absorb are the rare ones, and we've been adding carbon dioxide to that rare fraction for a century." He hesitated, because the honest part was next and honesty was slower. "What I can't tell you is exactly how much warming follows from exactly how many parts per million. That's the part the models fight about. I know the door and who gets in. I don't know how fast the room fills."

Ms. Sánchez considered him, keys still in her hand. "That's the first answer tonight that admitted what it didn't know," she said. "Lock up when you leave."

Eugenie pulled the last peanut butter cup from the bag and split it, handing him half. "Say the club sentence on the quiz."

He wrote it down, word for word, and underlined the trace gases twice, and outside the rain had started against the dome.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
Laura had claimed the carrel by the periodicals because it was the only one with an outlet, and because from there she could watch the front doors in case Rory actually showed up. She spread her materials across the desk: the assignment sheet, a printed transcript, two highlighters, and a legal pad already cross-hatched with abandoned arguments. Mr. Foster's instructions had been merciless. Each of them would argue both sides of a school speech case before the mock court on Thursday, petitioner and respondent, five minutes apiece, and he would be listening for whether they could hold two positions at once without collapsing into mush. "Anyone can be right," he had said. "I want to know if you can be fair."

The case he had assigned was fictional but modeled on real disputes, a student suspended for refusing to follow a school dress code she said was political. Laura's first instinct had been sympathy for the student, and her first draft had read like a manifesto. Reading it over the night before, she had been embarrassed by its certainty. She wanted to believe the First Amendment settled it, but she suspected that belief was lazy, and laziness was the one thing Mr. Foster always caught.

Rory came through the doors at four-twenty, towing a rolling backpack and looking truculent about it, jaw set as though the library itself had wronged him. He dropped into the chair across from her and pulled out a thick printout still warm from the copier. "I found it," he said. "The line. You know the one."

"I don't know the one."

"Everyone knows the one." He flipped pages until he found the passage he had starred in the margin. "Tinker. The black armband case. Nineteen sixty-nine. Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students don't shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." He said it with the satisfaction of a boy who had dug up treasure, and for a moment Laura understood why people got enraptured by court opinions, why whole careers were built on a single sentence someone wrote in a marble building fifty years ago. The line had weight. It sounded like a door swinging open.

She copied it onto her legal pad, word for word, then sat looking at it. "That's for our side," she said slowly. "For the student."

"Obviously."

"But if I have to argue the school's side too, then I have to argue against that line. Or around it." She turned the pad sideways, as if the problem would look different tilted. "How do you argue around the most famous sentence about student speech in the country?"

Rory shrugged and uncapped a pen with his teeth. "You say the armbands were quiet and the dress code isn't. You say Tinker protects expression that doesn't disrupt anything, and the school says this disrupts everything."

"That's not arguing around it, that's arguing it doesn't apply." She wrote both possibilities and drew an arrow between them, then another arrow back, because the arrow was a lie either way. The cases weren't cleanly separable. That was the trouble with the whole exercise. The student's lawyers would reach back to Tinker and say the schoolhouse gate had never been rebuilt; the school's lawyers would say the gate had simply moved, or that the corridor beyond it had grown louder and more dangerous than a corridor of armbands. Neither claim was exactly false.

Jessie found them twenty minutes later, carrying three coffees in a cardboard carrier despite the sign at the entrance, and slid into the seat beside Rory with the composure of someone who had decided not to care. "What are you two fighting about?"

"Utilitarianism," Rory said.

"We are not fighting about utilitarianism."

"You said, and I quote, 'the greatest good for the school community,' like four times."

"I said it once." But she had been thinking along those lines, that the respondent's whole architecture rested on consequences rather than principles, that the school's lawyers would count absences and disturbances and concluded that order was worth one girl's wardrobe. It was a coherent position. It was even, in some framings, a decent one. What unsettled her was that she could feel its decency most strongly at eleven at night, when she was tired and the respondent's brief was the one on top of the stack.

She tried an experiment aloud. "The record in Tinker was almost empty," she said. "No disruption, no fights, barely any comment. Seven justices looked at that and said the suspension couldn't stand. So maybe the line isn't a door. Maybe it's a scale, and what the Court actually said was: students keep their rights, and the school keeps its burden of proof." She looked up. "So for my respondent side, I don't attack the line. I concede it. I say the school carries its burden, and here is the record that meets it."

Jessie pulled the legal pad toward her and read the crossed-out drafts. "You've written 'the First Amendment is not absolute' like six times in different handwriting."

"It's true every time."

"It's true and it's a dodge," Jessie said, not unkindly. "You keep hiding behind it so you don't have to say what you actually think."

Laura opened her mouth to deny it and found nothing there. That was the honest inventory of the afternoon: she could now build both houses, brick for brick, and she still did not know which one she would choose to live in. She told them so. Rory said that was probably fine, that the whole point of arguing both sides was not knowing. She said she thought the point was supposed to be knowing better. They let the disagreement sit there between the coffees and the highlighted transcripts, unresolved, while the light through the tall windows went from white to gold.

Thursday evening, the library's community room had been arranged into a courtroom, folding chairs and a long table for the bench, and Mr. Foster sat at its center in his gray cardigan, entirely serious. Laura argued the student's side first and watched him nod once, at the schoolhouse gate line, delivered plainly, exactly as written. Then she switched, and argued the school, and conceded the line early, and built her record, and watched him nod once at that too. Afterward he gathered his notes and said it was the fairest pair of arguments he'd heard all night, and that she'd clearly decided the student was right and disguised it well in the second round. Laura thanked him. In the hallway, Jessie fell into step beside her and said, "He's wrong, you know. By the second argument I couldn't tell anymore." Laura stopped at the drinking fountain, filled a paper cone, and said, "Neither could I, and it's worse than that. Halfway through the respondent's rebuttal, I was winning."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
Eva had failed the first quiz, a 48 circled in red at the top of the page, and Ms. Bear had told her she could retake it Thursday if she could explain transcription and translation out loud, in her own words, without the diagram. That gave her four days.

On Monday she sat in the library with the textbook open to a page she had read six times without anything sticking. Elle dropped into the chair across from her and looked at the diagram of the cell with its arrows and labels.

"You still don't have it?" Elle said.

"I have it backwards. I keep thinking the DNA goes out to the ribosome itself, and it doesn't, and I don't understand why not."

"Farm thing," Elle said. Elle's family kept chickens and a stubborn pony, and she explained most of biology through the farm. "You don't take the whole filing cabinet out to the field. You photocopy the page you need."

Eva stared at her. "That's it?"

"That's what Alexe told me last year when I failed the same quiz. She's in the lab room now, actually."

They found Alexe at the back of the chemistry lab, rinsing beakers for Ms. Bear. Alexe was the kind of person who read the textbook the way other people read group chats, and she set down the beakers and came over when Eva explained the problem.

"Okay," Alexe said. "Walk me through what you know."

"The DNA stays in the nucleus." Eva said it slowly, testing it. "And something goes out. A copy of the gene."

"Which is what?"

"Messenger RNA. mRNA." She paused. "There's an enzyme that makes it."

"Name it."

Eva closed her eyes. She could see the label on the diagram, small print above the bubble of the nucleus. "RNA polymerase. It reads one strand of the DNA, the one strand, and it builds a matching strand of mRNA. And the mRNA carries the gene's instructions out." She opened her eyes. "To the ribosome. Where it gets translated into protein."

Alexe pointed at her with a wet beaker. "Say all of that again on Thursday and you'll pass."

"It can't be that easy."

"It's not easy, you just had it tangled. You were trying to make the DNA do the traveling."

That evening Eva called her little cousin, who was nine and had asked her at Thanksgiving what DNA actually did, and who had accepted "it's like a recipe" and then kept asking follow-up questions until Eva had given up and promised to explain someday. She did not tell him it was practice. She told him about the photocopy, and he wanted to know why the cell didn't just send the DNA itself, which was, she realized, exactly her own question from Monday.

"Because you need the original to stay safe," she said, standing in the kitchen with her mother chopping onions behind her. "The RNA polymerase reads one strand of the DNA and builds the matching mRNA, and the mRNA goes out carrying the instructions. The recipe stays in the kitchen. The copy gets greasy."

"Food gets made out of the copy?"

"Protein gets made out of the copy. Then the copy falls apart, and they make a new one if they need more."

Her cousin said "huh" in a tone that could either augur a career in molecular biology or mean he was already thinking about something else, probably Minecraft. She took it as a win either way.

On Thursday she sat across from Ms. Bear in the empty classroom at lunch, and Ms. Bear said, "Go," and Eva talked for ninety seconds without stopping: the DNA in the nucleus, the enzyme, the one strand read, the matching mRNA built, the instructions carried out, the ribosome, the protein. Ms. Bear wrote something on a sticky note and slid the retake across the desk. Eva got an 84, which felt, after the 48, like less of a triumph than a repair, a patched tire rather than a new one.

Walking out, she passed Elle in the hall. "How was it?" Elle asked.

"Better. I still couldn't tell you why the cell bothers with the enzyme instead of something simpler."

"Nobody asked you why. That's a question for someone who gets paid."

"Ms. Bear gets paid."

"Then ask her in office hours," Elle said, and shouldered her backpack toward the doors. "I have a pony to feed, and if you think translation is complicated, that animal has translated 'dinner' into about fourteen different sounds."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The sled drill was supposed to be simple: four boys, one weighted sled, twenty yards of torn turf. Dominic took his place at the front rope with Reece behind him and two others behind that, and when the coach blew the whistle they pushed, boots skidding, the sled's iron frame screaming along the ground. Afterward the coach held up his stopwatch and said nothing for a moment, which was worse than shouting.

"Keagan ran this thing solo Tuesday," he finally said. "Twenty yards, and I clocked him. Keagan, tell them what I clocked you at."

"Six flat," Keagan said, hands on his hips, still breathing hard.

"Six flat alone. Now the four of you together just ran it in nine. Four boys. Three extra seconds." He tossed the stopwatch from hand to hand. "I'm going to think about that. You run it again."

They ran it again, and it was worse, nine and change, because Reeace had gone to the back to hide where nobody could see whether his legs were really burning, and Dominic knew it, and the other two knew it too, and nobody said anything. That was the part that stayed with Dominic on the walk home, past the chain-link and the parking lot with its one flickering sodium lamp. It wasn't just that they were slower. It was that each of them, alone, would have been faster, and all four of them had chosen to be part of something slower.

That night he sat at the kitchen table collating what he could find, scrawling times in a notebook, hunting through the library's databases while his mother washed dishes behind him. He had expected nothing, some forum post about team chemistry maybe, so when the old paper came up he read the abstract twice. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had people pull on a rope and measured them, and when they pulled in a group each man pulled less hard than he did alone. Dominic sat back. It wasn't laziness and it wasn't a bad team. Somebody had measured it, over a hundred years ago, with a rope.

He wanted to tell someone immediately, and then he didn't, because he could already hear how it would sound. Hey, science says we're all slacking. Reece especially would take it as an accusation, and Reece took enough things as accusations already, ever since his demotion to second string. Dominic had learned to be careful around him, to check the weather before speaking. Some of the others just called Reece reactionary, dramatic, but Dominic thought it was more like a habit of self-defense, a door held shut with a foot behind it.

At Thursday practice he said nothing, and watched instead. The sled came out again, this time with the coach standing at the finish line with his stopwatch and his arms crossed, and again the group time crawled. But then, during the scrimmage that closed practice, Dominic watched Keagan chase a ball forty yards with a defender hanging on his shirt, and Keagan did not slow down, and the whole sideline was shouting, and nobody was measuring anything. Same boys. Same legs.

He stayed after to help gather the cones, folding the orange plastic into stacks while Ms. Andersen, who taught physics and kept the equipment shed in order, locked up the ball bags. He'd had her for a semester and she let silence happen, which was rare. So he asked her, almost casually, whether she'd heard of a French engineer with an unpronounceable name.

"Ringelmann," she said. "The rope experiments. Why?"

"Coach thinks we're dogging it on the sled."

"Are you?"

"That's the thing. I don't think so. But when Keagan pulls it alone he's faster than all four of us together. Ringelmann, 1913. That's a real finding, right? It's not just us."

She stacked the last cones on the rack. "It's a real finding," she said, and handed him the shed key to hang on its hook inside the door, and that was all, which was exactly why he'd asked her and not the coach.

The problem, he decided on the walk to the bus stop, was that the fact could be used two ways, and he wasn't sure which he believed. One way, it was an excuse: this is just how groups work, so the times don't mean we're cowards. The other way it was a warning: the pull drops off in a group, so the group owes itself something extra, some deliberate attention each boy has to add on purpose. His father, who managed a warehouse, would say the second without hesitating, and would probably say it over dinner tonight. But Dominic had watched Keagan sprint forty yards for a ball with nothing measured and nothing at stake except the shouting, and that pull had not dropped off at all, and Dominic could not make the two scenes agree with each other. Maybe the rope had nothing to do with soccer. Maybe watching had its own physics.

Friday, before the last sled run of the week, he gathered the four of them at the water station. "I looked something up," he said. "This engineer, Ringelmann, 1913. He had guys pull on a rope, and measured them, and in a group every guy pulled less hard than he did alone. Every time." He kept his voice level, kept it a fact and not a verdict. "I think it's happening to us."

"So we're weak," Reece said.

"I think we're normal. And I think we can decide to pull anyway."

They set up. Keagan moved to the front rope without being asked, and Dominic took the second position, and when the whistle came they drove, and the sled's runners shrieked, and somewhere in the middle of it Dominic heard Reece, behind him, making a sound like something being torn. The coach didn't say the time. He just looked at his stopwatch for a long moment, then clicked it back to zero and said, "Once more," and the four of them turned the sled around.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing.
story:
Nevaeh clocked out at nine and did not go straight home. She took the two folded leases to the break room, spread them on the table beside the vending machine, and looked at them the way you look at a math test you already suspect you failed. She had worked at Fairway for eleven months, Tuesdays and Thursdays and most Saturdays, and after her last paycheque she had done the arithmetic so many times the numbers had begun to feel like furniture, permanent and unmovable.

The first apartment, the one on Clarendon, charged nine hundred and eighty a month with heat and water included. The second, above the pawnshop on Miller Street, was eight hundred and sixty, but the listing said tenant pays all utilities, and when she had called, the landlord had estimated electric at "maybe a hundred, hundred and forty, depends on the season." Depends on the season. She wrote that phrase on a napkin and underlined it twice.

Hudson came in for his closing shift and dropped his apron on the chair across from her. "You're still doing the apartment thing."

"Utilities make it complicated." She turned the napkin toward him. "The cheap one might not be cheap."

"Everything's like that," Hudson said. "The sticker price and then the real price. Like cereal. Look at the cereal aisle sometime. The big box is per-ounce more than the small box." He was tying his apron while he said it, already halfway out the door of the conversation, and she understood that this was a thing she would now notice forever, the gap between the label and the truth of a thing.

She added the Miller Street numbers in the margin of the lease. Eight sixty plus a hundred and forty was a thousand even, before internet, before anything going wrong. Clarendon's nine eighty suddenly looked different, closer to honest. She tried to metabolize the shift, the way the apartment she had wanted, the one with the exposed brick and the bus stop outside, had quietly become the worse deal while she wasn't looking.

But the rent was only half the question, and she knew it, because last Sunday she had looked up her income. Fourteen fifty a month, roughly, after tax, if she picked up the extra Saturday shifts and nothing went wrong. She had found a page on her phone, some federal thing, and read it three times: in the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing. Thirty percent of her income was four hundred and thirty-five dollars. Both apartments were more than double that, with utilities or without, and she had sat with the phone in her hand feeling something seismic rearrange itself under her plans, small and enormous at once.

Ms. Russo, who did her shopping late to avoid the crowds and always came through Nevaeh's till with the same coupon folder, appeared at the break room door with a basket of reduced-price bread. "Still here, sweetheart?"

"Trying to figure out apartments," Nevaeh said. "Did you know there's a thing where if your housing is more than thirty percent of your income, they call you cost-burdened? The government has a whole word for it."

"Cost-burdened," Ms. Russo repeated, tasting it. "My daughter was that for years. Half her paycheque went to a landlord in a building with a flooded basement." She set her basket down. "You're not moving out alone, are you?"

"With Ireland, maybe. She's asking her mom tonight." That was the other variable, the one that didn't fit in any margin. Ireland had a job at the library that paid less than Fairway but steadier hours, and if her mother said yes, thirty percent of their combined income might actually cover Clarendon. Might. Depends on the season, and on the mother, and on whether Ireland meant it when she said she was serious, because Ireland said a lot of things with her whole chest and then reconsidered them quietly, later, and Nevaeh had learned to wait before believing the first version.

Ms. Russo picked up her basket, then paused. "My cousin rents out the flat over on Clarendon. The one over the dress shop. Heat included." She said it lightly, the way you mention a thing you could take back. Nevaeh felt the napkin numbers tremble in her head, eight hundred and sixty, nine hundred and eighty, thirty percent, the whole careful structure swaying toward a door she hadn't known existed.

"Can I text you about it?" Nevaeh asked, already pulling out her phone.

Ms. Russo laughed and recited her number, and Nevaeh typed it in twice to be sure, the way she had checked the arithmetic, the way she would check everything now.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is 50,000 pounds or more.
story:
The laundromat on Marsh Street had two working dryers and a folding table with a coin slot on its side, as though the table itself might need washing. Naomi spread her mother's old notebook on the table, smoothed it flat, and set the two leases side by side: one from the flat on Cavendish Road, one from the bedsit above the chip shop. She had come here to wash her school uniform because their machine at home had died on Tuesday, and somewhere between the spin cycle and the rinse she had decided this was the only place she would ever get the arithmetic done.

London came in with a pillowcase of socks and dropped onto the bench beside her, stretching like a cat. "You brought homework to a laundromat."

"It's not homework." Naomi slid the Cavendish lease across. "I'm moving out. Maybe. If the numbers work."

"You're seventeen."

"I'll be eighteen in June, and Mum's moving to her sister's in September, and I am not moving to a village where the bus comes on Thursdays." She tapped the paper. "Cavendish Road is seven hundred a month but bills are included. The bedsit is six twenty-five but you pay electricity and water on top, and I have to guess how much that is."

London picked up the bedsit lease and read it with the slow suspicion of someone decoding a foreign language. "What's this bit, 'deposit equivalent to eight weeks' rent'?"

"That's the problem." Naomi pulled the notebook closer. On the top of the page she had written the numbers in two columns, and beneath them a running list of questions her own brain kept refusing to answer. "Eight weeks on six twenty-five is a lot of money. Like, over a thousand pounds. And I keep thinking, that can't be right, because I read something once, in that housing leaflet at the library, about there being a limit."

The dryer thumped its final load and nobody moved to empty it. Calum appeared at the door with a duffel bag and a plant, an actual small fern, which he set on top of a washer as if it needed the ride. "The landlord above the chip shop asked for eight weeks?" he said, having evidently heard everything through the propped door. "Mine only asked for five. We're on the same street, basically."

"That's because yours is legal," Naomi said, and even as she said it she felt the ground shift under her, because she had not known that a second ago. Five weeks. The leaflet had said something about five weeks. She found the folded page in her backpack, the one she'd taken from the library rack out of boredom during a fire drill, and opened it on the table between London's socks and Calum's fern.

In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is fifty thousand pounds or more. She read it twice. Six twenty-five a month was seven thousand five hundred a year, nowhere near the threshold, so five weeks was the ceiling, and eight weeks was three weeks past it. Three weeks of wages from her Saturday job, roughly, sitting in the landlord's account for no reason except that nobody her age ever pushed back.

"You look like you caught something," London said.

"I caught him." Naomi laughed, and the laugh had an edge of disbelief in it. "He's over the limit. It's capped, it's the law, and he either doesn't know or he's betting I don't."

"Be circumspect, though," Calum said, watering his fern from a bottle he'd apparently brought for the purpose. "He can just refuse to rent to you. There's no law that says he has to like being corrected by someone with a fern-having friend."

Naomi started a new column in the notebook, slower this time. The truth was she had been treating this like a maths problem where the answer lived somewhere outside her, in the numbers, waiting to be found. But the numbers only told her what each flat cost. They didn't tell her what her life would predicate itself on: the chip shop bedsit was cheap and illegal in its deposit and fifteen minutes from everything, and Cavendish Road was expensive and safe and lonely, out where the streets went quiet like a steppe after dark, flat and pale and stretching toward nothing she recognized.

She added up the utilities estimate she'd got from asking the cashier at the corner shop, who paid the same company. Six twenty-five plus roughly ninety for bills came to seven fifteen, near enough. Cavendish at seven hundred, all in, was actually cheaper, which annoyed her in a way she couldn't fully justify.

"So which one?" London said, gathering her socks into a shape that suggested she had never once folded anything.

Naomi looked at the two columns, at the deposit she could now name as over the cap and the flat she could actually afford and the one she wanted and couldn't. "I'm going to tell the chip shop man his deposit breaks the law," she said. "And if he says no, I'll take Cavendish Road and eat a lot of rice."

"That's not an answer, that's two answers."

"It's both of them," Naomi said, and closed the notebook, and slid it into her backpack next to the library leaflet, which she decided she was not returning.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water.
story:
The vet clinic smelled like bleach and wet dog, and Ava had been there for two hours with her flashcards, waiting for Mr. Ramos to finish sewing up her cat. Feivel had swallowed part of a shoelace, which the intake form had required her to transliterate from her mother's Russian, since her mother's English abandoned her precisely in emergencies. The receptionist had squinted at "nyitochnaya tsepochka" until Ava said "it's a drawstring," and the receptionist had said, "Honey, the cat doesn't care what language it was."

She cared, though. That was the problem. The exam was Monday, cellular respiration, and no matter how many times she copied the arrows, glucose to pyruvate to the tiny furnaces, the whole thing refused to become anything she could picture. She had the vocabulary without the world. She knew the word "enthalpy" from a practice problem and could not have said what it felt like, which seemed to her the difference between passing and understanding.

Her phone buzzed. Louis-Felix, from the study group she'd abandoned: "we're at the diner, jeremiah bought everyone fries with his financial aid refund, your seat is getting cold." She typed "vet, cat, dying, not literally" and put the phone face down. Last month she'd done the opposite. Flashback: the Sunday before the anatomy test, her friends had dragged her to the boardwalk, and she'd gone, and she'd failed the anatomy test by two points, and Jeremiah had said, gently, that two points was the price of a ferris wheel, and she had not spoken to him for a day because he was right in a way she couldn't argue with.

"Miss?" said a vet tech in green scrubs, leaning over the desk. "Your cat's out of surgery. You can go back when Dr. Patel's done with the intake notes. Could be twenty minutes."

Twenty minutes. Ava looked at her flashcards, all arrows and abbreviations, and thought about the oxygen line on the diagram, the one she'd memorized without ever reading it. She walked to the back hallway because the tech had left the door open, and because she wanted to see the anesthesia machine, the tanks bolted to the wall with their labels.

Mr. Ramos, who lived two houses down and whose dog her mother fed when he traveled, was sitting on a stool by the recovery cages, waiting on his own animal, a spaniel with a bandaged paw. "Ava," he said. "Feivel?"

"Drawstring," she said. "He's fine. Mr. Ramos, can I ask you something weird? The oxygen in those tanks. Where does it go? In the animal, I mean. Does it just, like, circulate?"

He rubbed the spaniel's ear and considered. "That's more your department than mine. I fix bones. But the tech was explaining the monitors earlier, because I asked the same thing. Apparently the blood carries it to the cells, and in the cells, in these little membrane folds, it's the final acceptor. Takes the electrons at the end of the line and combines with the protons to make water."

"Water," Ava said.

"That's what she said. The oxygen we breathe turns into water inside us. I thought she was joking. She wasn't joking."

Ava sat down on the folding chair beside him. The electron transport chain, the diagram she'd redrawn eleven times, was not an abstraction floating somewhere near the word "mitochondria." It sat in the inner membrane, an actual place, and at the end of its line oxygen stood waiting to take electrons and bind protons, and the product was the same water in the dog's water bowl, in her own blood. She breathed in, and some fraction of that breath would end up, before dark, as water. Every breath a small hydrology.

"That's the thing I've been staring at for two days," she said. "I had it on a flashcard. Final electron acceptor. I would have written it on the exam and not known one single thing about it." She laughed, a little embarrassed. "I might still fail. Knowing where it happens isn't the same as knowing how."

"Probably not," Mr. Ramos agreed. "Knowing where things happen is what I do, though, and it's not nothing."

The tech appeared in the doorway. "Feivel's waking up. He's grumpy, which is normal."

Ava stood, and on her way past the anesthesia tanks she put her palm flat against the cold metal, the way you'd touch a horse. In her pocket her phone buzzed again, the study group, the fries, the seat going cold, and she decided she would text Louis-Felix the whole thing, the oxygen and the water, before Monday, and let them tell her whether she'd gotten it right.

"Come on, Feivel," she said to the carrier. "Let's go breathe."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
The car was a seven-year-old hatchback the colour of a rain cloud, and it sat in the back row of the lot under a string of plastic flags that snapped in the wind. Maria had walked past the dealership every day for two weeks on her way home from school, and every day the car seemed to be waiting for her personally, which she knew was a trick of the lighting and did not care. Sixteen with a licence and no car meant asking her mother for rides, and her mother's shifts at the hospital began at six, which meant the bus, which meant forty minutes each way, which meant she had done the math so many times the numbers had worn a groove in her head.

The price on the windshield said 4,900. She had 1,340 in a shoebox, and 212 more in a savings account her grandmother had opened when Maria was nine, an account that had somehow grown to 212 from an original 200 without anyone touching it. When she'd asked the bank teller about this, the woman had said, "Interest," in the tone of someone naming a small weather event, and moved on to the next customer.

She brought Salma on Saturday for the moral support and because Salma's father bought cars for a living and she claimed to know things. Darwin came because he had nothing else to do and because he was the closest thing their friend group had to an iconoclast, suspicious of anything advertised with flags. The salesman was named Rick, and his handshake lasted slightly too long.

"Great little runner," Rick said of the hatchback. "Now, if you're short on the full amount, we do financing right here." He led them toward a glass office where a woman named Ms. Whitaker sat with a calculator shaped like a credit card, a promotional item the size of a serving tray. Ms. Whitaker had the calm of someone who had adjudicated a thousand disputes between people and their own money, and she laid out the terms without smiling at anybody, which Maria found oddly reassuring.

The terms were these: if Maria put down her 1,340 and financed the rest, she would pay it back over three years, and the total would come to more than 3,560, which was more than the 3,560 she owed, more by an amount Ms. Whitaker called "the cost of borrowing." Maria looked at the number and felt something in her go quiet and careful. The car would cost the car plus something. She thought of her grandmother's account, growing in the dark like a plant on a windowsill nobody watered, and of this, the same force pointed the other way, and she understood that interest was not a fee exactly but a direction. Money moved, and it mattered which way.

"So I could finance it," Maria said slowly, "or I could wait and save the rest."

"That's the shape of it," Ms. Whitaker said, and did not push. Rick pushed. Rick talked about building credit history, about established responsibility, about how nobody her age paid cash for anything. Darwin, examining a brochure as though it might contain evidence, said, "He means nobody her age has cash."

Outside, while Rick went to check on a trade-in, Salma sat on the hood of a nearby sedan until a manager frowned her off it, and the three of them stood by the hatchback. Maria took out her phone and opened the banking app, where her first credit card bill was waiting. She'd gotten the card two months ago for emergencies, and had used it for a coat, a textbook, and a birthday present for her cousin, and the balance was 143. The app offered her a choice in two buttons. One said Pay Minimum: 15. The other said Pay Full Balance: 143.

"Pay the minimum," Salma said immediately. "That's what the button is for. Fifteen dollars, and you still have 128 for the car."

"But then interest starts," Maria said.

"On 128 dollars? That's nothing."

Darwin, who had been reading over her shoulder with the expression he wore when he suspected the world of fine print, said, "My sister did this. She paid the minimum and then interest showed up on stuff she'd already bought. It's the grace period. If you pay the full balance by the due date each month, you don't get charged interest on new purchases at all. She says the whole thing is a game where the card company bets you'll only pay the minimum."

"Then I pay the full balance," Maria said.

"That's 143 out of your car money," Salma said. "The car is 4,900. That's like four months of bus rides."

They argued about it in the flat wind of the lot, flags cracking overhead, while somewhere behind the glass Rick was presumably describing them to a colleague as hot prospects. Salma said the minimum existed for people in her exact situation; Darwin said the minimum existed for the card company's exact situation. Maria stood between them holding her phone with both hands, and what she kept coming back to was not the 143 but the principle underneath it, that the card was free if she was whole and expensive if she was partial, and that the whole question of the car was the same question stretched longer. Borrowing was renting money. Saving was renting it out. Her grandmother's 212 had been doing quiet work for seven years, and Rick's three-year plan would do the same work against her.

She paid the 143. Then she walked back into the office, where Ms. Whitaker looked up from her enormous calculator, and asked whether the dealership would hold the hatchback for two weeks. Ms. Whitaker said they couldn't hold, but she could write Maria's name on the file and if the car sold, it sold. Maria thought about that for a moment, about the turbid little pool of wanting that had carried her here every day for two weeks, and found it was clearer now, or at least she could see the bottom of it.

"Write my name," she said.

Ms. Whitaker uncapped her pen. Outside, Salma pressed her face to the glass and gave a thumbs-up, and Darwin took a photo of the hatchback, and Maria watched the letters of her own name appear on the folder one stroke at a time.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament.
story:
Ms. Çelik had pushed the desks into a horseshoe and taped a paper sign to the front table that read PARLIAMENT, and by the second week of the model parliament Layla understood that the sign was the only easy part. The class had voted for a bill to cap the price of period products in shops, and Layla, whose idea it had been, had assumed the hard part would be convincing people. She was wrong about that, and being wrong was starting to feel like the theme of the whole exercise.

The first draft was hers, one paragraph written on her phone the night before. "Period products shall be affordable for all," it said, and Quinn, reading it aloud in a flat voice, asked what "affordable" meant to a shopkeeper in a courtroom. Rory pointed out that "products" could include anything from tampons to decorative candles if a lawyer felt like arguing it. Nobody was being cruel. That was the uncomfortable part. They were only doing the thing properly, and the thing done properly kept swallowing her sentence whole.

"Real government bills don't start like this," Ms. Çelik said from the window, not looking up from her marking. "They start with lawyers." Layla asked what she meant, and Ms. Çelik only said that the students should find out for themselves by Thursday, because that was the sort of teacher she was. That night Layla sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open while her mother watched something with the sound low, and she read that in the United Kingdom, government bills were drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament. She read it twice. There was a whole office, a staff of lawyers, whose entire job was turning what politicians wanted into words precise enough to survive committee. Even the people with the big ideas handed the writing over to specialists, and then argued about what came back.

She brought printouts the next morning. "So we're the ministers with the idea," she said, spreading them on the desk between Quinn and Rory, "and we also have to be the Parliamentary Counsel, because there's no one else." Quinn frowned at the phrase, then at her draft. "Then we write it like lawyers. Every term defined, every duty on someone." Rory, who had spent the summer shelving stock at a pharmacy, said the shops would just pass costs on to suppliers unless the bill bound them too, and Layla felt the problem widen like a crack under pressure. Her paragraph had wanted to protect people. The draft they spent forty minutes building mostly assigned obligations, and it read like something designed by someone who distrusted everyone involved, which, she had to admit, was the point.

Committee was worse, in a useful way. Ms. Çelik appointed three students to tear the bill apart clause by clause, and they did it with a diligence that made Layla's ears go hot. A boy she didn't know well raised the clause limiting prices and asked what happened to small shops whose margins were already thin, whether the bill would subjugate one group's hardship to another's, and Quinn, to Layla's surprise, said maybe it would, and that they should say so in the preamble instead of pretending the trade-off didn't exist. Layla had wanted to object that the trade-off wasn't the same as the injustice, but the sentence stalled in her mouth, because she wasn't sure it was true, and saying things she wasn't sure of as if they were certain was exactly what the drafting exercise had taught her to stop doing.

The debate came the following Tuesday, and it moved her in a direction she hadn't predicted. She stood to open and found herself arguing for a clause she had originally resisted, an amendment letting shops apply for relief if the cap caused hardship, because Rory's pharmacy stories had worked on her the way evidence is supposed to. Someone on the other side accused the amendment of being subterfuge, a loophole dressed as compassion, and Layla heard the accusation land and had to admit, standing there, that it might be half right. The bill was trying to do two things at once, relieve a burden and prevent a dodge, and every word she'd drafted pulled in one direction or the other.

The vote was close. Eleven to nine in favour on second reading, and then the third reading, and then Ms. Çelik, playing the monarch with visible enjoyment, gave the royal assent and rapped the whiteboard marker on the desk like a sceptre. The class laughed, and Quinn stood and shook Layla's hand with mock solemnity, and someone had made a paper crown.

After the bell Layla stayed behind to stack the chairs, because Ms. Çelik had asked and because she wasn't ready to let the room turn back into a normal classroom. On the board, half erased, the bill still existed, clauses and subclauses, her handwriting and Rory's and Quinn's overlapping. "It's not what I wanted it to be," she said. Ms. Çelik considered the board. "It rarely is. The wanting and the writing are different jobs." Layla looked at the clause about relief for small shops, the one she still couldn't decide was compassionate or noxious, and picked up the eraser, and stood there holding it without moving.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide.
story:
Alexis sat on the floor of the clinic's back room with a biology textbook open on her knees and a sleeping beagle against her hip. Saturdays were supposed to be her shift for cleaning kennels and refilling water bowls, but Mr. Wilson had caught her studying at the front desk during a slow hour and told her she could review back there, as long as she answered the phone if it rang. That had been two weeks before her exam, and now it was three days.

The problem was the diagrams. Glycolysis she could manage, glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, a modest payout of ATP. But after that the map dissolved into arrows and abbreviations, and every time she tried to hold the whole route in her head, it slid apart like wet paper. She had told Keira at lunch that it was hopeless, and Keira, who was applying to seven colleges and kept a color-coded planner, had offered to quiz her. Lincoln had overheard and invited himself along, which was how the three of them ended up in the clinic waiting room on a rainy Saturday, using the good chairs, while Alexis straightened magazines between questions.

"What comes after glycolysis," Keira read from her notes, and Lincoln, phlegmatic as ever, leaned back and said, "The mitochondria," as if that settled everything. Alexis said it didn't, because the mitochondria had an outer membrane and an inner membrane and a matrix, and the pyruvate had to get somewhere specific before anything else happened, and she could not remember where, or what it became when it arrived.

"Acetyl-CoA," Lincoln said. "It becomes acetyl-CoA. And it releases, um." He rubbed his jaw. "Something."

"Water," Keira guessed.

"Water comes way later," Alexis said. "Electron transport." She could feel the answer circling somewhere outside her reach, the way a word you know sits on the tip of your tongue. Keira argued that the first carbon dioxide had to come from the Krebs cycle, because that was where the textbook drew the little CO2 bubbles thick as suds, four of them per glucose, and Lincoln said no, it was earlier, it was the step before, and the two of them got louder until a woman in the waiting area looked up from her carrier and they all dropped their voices.

Alexis closed her eyes and tried to walk the route herself, the way she had learned to do during a dull Tuesday the week before, when Mr. Wilson had let her watch him place an IV line in a dehydrated cat. He had narrated the whole time, calm and steady, and what she remembered afterward was not the catheter but his habit of asking where exactly the fluid was going. Everything moved along a path, he had said, and if you lost the path, you lost the patient. Glucose, she thought. Cytoplasm. Two pyruvates. Then a door, a crossing, and then.
