"In the matrix," she said, opening her eyes. "It happens in the mitochondrial matrix. Each pyruvate gets converted into acetyl-CoA, and that step releases one molecule of carbon dioxide. One. Per pyruvate. So before the Krebs cycle even starts, before all those bubbles Keira loves, the first CO2 is already out." She had not known she knew it until she said it, and there was a strange, provisional satisfaction in that, as though she had put a foot on ice and only afterward felt it hold.

Keira looked it up. Her phone screen glowed between them. "Matrix," she confirmed, and Alexis watched her friend's face move from skepticism through something almost rueful toward the particular frustration of someone whose erudition has been outrun. "You got it backwards," she told Lincoln, but not unkindly, and Lincoln shrugged, because being wrong had never seemed to vilify him in his own eyes the way it vilified Keira in hers. Alexis recognized both positions. She had spent most of the semester being Keira about it, treating every wrong answer as a verdict on her intelligence, and only lately, sitting on the clinic floor with a beagle breathing against her ribs, had she begun to think that maybe Lincoln's ease and Keira's rigor were not opposites but tools, and that a person could hold one in each hand.

The phone rang. Alexis answered it the way Mr. Wilson had taught her, clinic name, her name, how can I help, and a man asked whether they took turtles, and she said she would check, and covered the receiver. Mr. Wilson appeared from the exam room, wiping his hands, and said they did, tell him to bring it in before four. He glanced at the textbook splayed open on the chair, at Keira's notes, at Lincoln doodling a mitochondrion in the margin of a consent form, and something in his dry, tired face suggested approval, though he said nothing about it.

They stayed until the turtle arrived, a box turtle with a cracked shell, carried in a laundry basket by a boy maybe nine years old. Alexis watched Mr. Wilson's hands, the same steadiness as with the cat, and found herself thinking, without meaning to, of the route inside her own body, glucose dividing, pyruvate crossing, carbon dioxide leaving one molecule at a time in the dark of the matrix. It did not feel like memorization anymore. It felt like something happening, quietly, in everything alive, including the turtle and the boy and the woman still waiting with her carrier.

She still was not sure she could reproduce the whole diagram on Monday. The link reaction had clicked, but the Krebs cycle was still mostly fog, and electron transport was a rumor she had only heard about. She said so on the walk to the bus stop, and Keira said that was honest at least, and Lincoln said the fog was where the learning happened, which sounded like something off a poster, and Alexis laughed at him for it, and Keira said, "Quiz me on Krebs," and pulled out her notes under the streetlight.

"The first compound after acetyl-CoA enters," Keira began, and Alexis, with the beagle's warmth still somehow at her hip, said, "Citrate. It's citrate," and Keira wrote it down.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: In a LEFT JOIN, putting a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total > 0, removes the NULL rows and makes it act like an inner join.
story:
The shop smelled of isopropyl alcohol and the burnt-sugar ghost of someone's lunch, and Alyssa had decided she loved it, which was probably an exaggeration but she held onto it anyway. Ms. Chukwu let her use the back counter on Saturdays, a laptop propped between a bin of cracked screens and the till, on the condition that she "make herself useful." Useful meant the customer list. Ms. Chukwu kept two files, one of every customer who had ever walked in, and one of the repair orders, and after three years the files had drifted apart like friends who stop texting.

"Find me the people who never came back," Ms. Chukwu had said, in the tone she used for things that were obviously simple. "Before the rent review. I want to call them, or at least know their names."

Alyssa had been teaching herself SQL for six weeks, partly for the college application she'd described as "a personal project in databases," which was true the way a photo of your best angle is you. Laurie, who worked the front counter and was repeating senior year, had laughed at her notebooks full of diagrams until Laurie stopped laughing and started asking questions instead, and Alyssa had pretended not to notice that this felt like the best thing that had happened all autumn.

She wrote the join on Saturday with Laurie leaning over her shoulder, close enough that Alyssa could hear the little click of Laurie's tongue stud against her teeth. "Left join customers to orders," Alyssa said, typing. "Then the customers with no orders show up with blanks." The query ran. Forty-one names came back, each with empty columns where an order should have been, and Alyssa sat very still because it had worked, actually worked, the way things in books worked.

But forty-one was too many. Ms. Chukwu, sorting screws into trays, said half of those people had bought screen protectors at least, trivial things, and she didn't want to phone a man about his loyalty when he'd only ever spent eight dollars. So Alyssa added one filter, where orders.total > 0, to keep the real buyers out, and ran it again, confident, already half-imagining the telling of this at her interview in January. The result came back empty. Not forty-one names, not ten names, nothing at all, a blank grid staring back like a locked door. She ran it three more times, the way you press a button harder when the machine ignores you.

"That's not sad," Laurie said, when Alyssa made a sound she would later describe as not a sound. "Watch what you changed." They looked at the two queries side by side, Laurie's finger hovering, never quite touching the screen. Alyssa read the line aloud: where orders.total > 0. Then she read the output again, all those NULLs from the first run, the customers whose order columns were blank. The filter was sweeping them out with the rest. "It kills the NULL rows," she said slowly. "Put a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, and the left join just acts like an inner join." Laurie said "huh" in a way that made it clear she'd understood maybe half, and that was somehow better than if she'd understood all of it. Alyssa moved the condition into the ON clause, ran it, and the forty-one names returned, unfiltered, whole, exactly as before, plus the eighty-three people who had bought something. She had not solved the problem Ms. Chukwu actually had. She had only learned why she couldn't solve it yet.

Yara arrived near closing with a phone in a sock, its screen spidered, and asked Laurie for a quote, and asked Alyssa, with a classmate's flat kindness, how the "database thing" was going. Alyssa said it was going well, which was true and wasn't. The erudition she had been accumulating all term, the diagrams, the vocabulary she'd used like a coat against the cold, had turned out to be one long desensitize, she realized on the bus home, the window fogging and clearing against her sleeve: she had grown comfortable not understanding things, fluent in the shape of an inchoate plan. Tonight something had gone blunt and real instead. The query had refused her, and then taught her, and the cost was that the list Ms. Chukwu wanted, the small spenders filtered from the true ghosts, still didn't exist, and the rent review was Thursday.

She texted Laurie from the bus: the NULLs are the whole point. The three dots appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. At the shop, in her mind, Ms. Chukwu was already picking up the phone and dialing all forty-one names, though Alyssa knew she hadn't, knew she was only sorting screws, waiting, holding the shop together the way she always had, with or without the answer.

Laurie's reply came as the bus turned onto her street: "come tuesday. bring the laptop. also yara says hi."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
Xavier had agreed to volunteer at the food bank because his mother had signed the form before he got home, which he understood to be a kind of preempt against argument, and because the garden attached to it was, according to the flyer, in need of hands. He arrived at nine on a Saturday and was handed a clipboard by a woman named Ms. Nikolaidis, who pointed at a row of raised beds and said the zucchini had opinions. He took this to mean something horticultural and did not ask.

Inside the packing room, his schoolmates Anjali and Jamal were already assembling hampers on a long steel table. Jamal had a spreadsheet open on his phone, tracking his hours with the seriousness of a man guarding a border. He needed forty for a scholarship application, and he mentioned this twice in the first ten minutes, then once more for anyone who had been in the washroom. Anjali, by contrast, moved down the table without explanation, filling boxes as if she had been born mid-task.

Xavier was given the baby food. His job was to check dates on jars of purée and slide one into any hamper marked with a blue dot, plus a sleeve of crackers shaped like fish if the dot had a star beside it. He had expected cans of soup, the dull arithmetic of tins. Instead he found himself reaching for the blue dots constantly, so constantly that he started keeping count on the back of a receipt, a tally that grew faster than he would have guessed.

"These are all kids," he said finally, holding up a hamper with two dots and a star.

"Visits, technically," Anjali said, not looking up. "Children accounted for about a third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report." She said it the way other people recited bus schedules, flat and certain, and then added, "I read it for a civics thing," which was as much biography as she offered anyone.

Jamal leaned over to inspect Xavier's tally. "You're counting by hand? There's an app for that." There was, apparently, an app for everything, and Jamal had opinions on all of them. What Jamal did not have was a position on the tally itself, and Xavier noticed that his friend's attention slid off the number the way water slides off wax, settling instead on his phone, where hour six of forty was logging itself into eternity.

Xavier kept packing. He had come in with a theory, half-formed on the bus, that volunteering was mostly extrinsic, a line on a form, a transaction dressed in better clothes, and Jamal's spreadsheet had so far supported it beautifully. But the tally on the receipt was doing something to the theory. He tried to hold both ideas at once, the way you hold two grocery bags, and found they didn't cancel each other so much as lean. It was possible the spreadsheet and the blue dots were both true, and possible that he had no idea yet what he thought about that, and he was surprised by how little this bothered him.

Ms. Nikolaidis came through with a crate of tomatoes from the garden, the ones Xavier had weeded around an hour earlier without knowing where they were going. She set the crate down beside Anjali and said, "Those are the last of the determinates, so thank whoever watered them," and left before anyone could be thanked, which struck Xavier as a private kind of probity, credit refused at the door.

At noon the hampers went out to the cars, and Xavier watched a boy about seven carry the fish-shaped crackers to a sedan with the care of a boy carrying a bird. Jamal photographed his spreadsheet for the scholarship portal. Anjali washed the steel table without being asked.

"We're back next Saturday," she said, drying her hands. "Six of those dots were yours."

Jamal looked up from his phone. "I'll be at nine and a quarter," he said. "I'm pacing myself."

Xavier folded the receipt with the tally on it and put it in his back pocket, then went out to the garden to see whether the zucchini had changed their opinions.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
The art shed at Camp Kettleworth smelled of turpentine and pine sap, and the screen door clapped shut behind Morgan every time she came through it, so that everyone knew she had arrived before she said a word. She spread her nine finished prints across the long table like a hand of cards. Rania leaned over them with a popsicle dripping orange onto her wrist.

"They're all you," Rania said. "Every single one."

"That's the theme." Morgan squared the edges. "Self-portrait. Ten pictures, one statement, the whole portfolio due at the end of August." The statement was due first, actually, on Friday, one page, and she had written nothing but her name.

Wyatt pulled a chair around backwards and sat with his arms folded on its back. He tapped the third print, the one where Morgan had braided her hair over one shoulder and turned her face to the window light. "This one's my favorite. But if I put them all in a stack, I can't tell which is which. You look like you in all of them. Same expression. Like you're waiting for something."

"I am waiting. For the tenth picture." She said it lightly, but it sat in her stomach differently, the way a sky that is merely gray can, by late afternoon, begin to portend rain. Nine days of work. Nine versions of her own face, each one careful, each one the same.

That night she borrowed Ms. Grant's art books, the heavy ones kept behind the supply cage, and carried them to her bunk by flashlight because lights-out was at ten. She was looking for anything on portraiture when she found the photographs: small, black-and-white, a woman in a blonde wig at a kitchen counter, the same woman as a housewife clutching a collar, the same woman as a hitchhiker on a road. Morgan turned the pages slowly, counting before she read the caption.

"Rania," she whispered across the cabin, waking her. "Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy photographs, black and white, all of herself, posed as characters from imaginary movies."

"So they're self-portraits," Rania mumbled into her pillow.

"No. That's the thing. She's not being herself in any of them. Seventy pictures and she's a different invented person every time, from films that were never made." Morgan kept her voice low. "They're all her and none of them are her."

In the morning she took the tenth sheet of film and walked past the lake, past the canoe rack, to the cluster of birches behind the dining hall where the mist had not yet burned off. She had brought her mother's old raincoat from the lost-and-found bin and a scarf that smelled faintly of someone else's lavender. She set the tripod in the wet grass, wrapped the scarf over her hair, and looked at the camera the way she imagined a stranger would, a woman waiting at the edge of a road in a place she had never been. The shutter clicked, and the mist drifted through the trees behind her, and a crow called somewhere and was answered.

When she developed it in the shed, Wyatt and Rania stood at her shoulders while the image surfaced in the tray, gray shapes resolving into a figure no one recognized at first. "Who's that?" Wyatt said, and then, quieter, "Oh."

Morgan laid the tenth print beside the other nine and understood, finally, what had been wrong. She had spent the summer taking pictures of a girl who looked like her honest self, steady and waiting, and she had called that a theme. The truthful theme was something else: not who she was, but the many people she might invent, the selves no one had assigned her. She would have to start over, and there were eleven days left.

She wrote the statement that afternoon at the picnic table, three quarters of a page, crossing out "exploring identity" as too vague, once writing something vitriolic about her own first nine photographs and then softening it, because the pictures had not lied exactly; they had only told one small truth and called it the whole. Rania read it over her shoulder and pointed at a line. "You say here you're not sure which version of you is the real one. Won't Ms. Grant mark you down for that?"

"Maybe," Morgan said. She folded the page and put it in her back pocket. In the shed, she pinned the tenth print to the corkboard, the woman in the scarf half turned toward the birches, and began mixing a fresh tray of developer for the eleven blank sheets waiting in the box.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The article was in German, and Payton had fifteen minutes left before she had to stand at the front of Room 214 and summarize it aloud. The teacher, Mr. Chukwu, had handed out photocopies at the start of the period: a short news piece from a regional paper, three paragraphs, dense type. She had done what she always did with a difficult text, started at the bottom, at the last paragraph, where the sentences were shorter and she could pick out words she knew. Kirche, Wasser, something about a committee. She was halfway through building a translation in the margin of her notebook when she realized the clock had eaten nine of her twenty minutes.

Across the table, Aicha was already mouthing her summary, her article face down, fingers stilled on the desktop. Arjun had his copy turned sideways, annotating fast, but from the top, Payton noticed. From the very top, the first paragraph, where the longest and most complicated sentences lived. She watched him underline the opening line twice, and something about his certainty bothered her, the way he treated the first paragraph as if it were the whole assignment.

"Why are you starting there?" she whispered. "That's the hardest part."

"Because it's the most important part." He didn't look up. "Mr. Chukwu told us last week. Most news articles use the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story."

"Then what's the ending for?"

"Details. Stuff they could cut." He tapped her paper. "You're decoding the decoration and skipping the building."

She stared at her margin notes, nine minutes of work on what might be the equivalent of the footnotes, and felt the whole shape of her plan tilt. If Arjun was right, she had been reading the article back to front, literally. She had to recalibrate, and fast: she flipped back to the first paragraph, laid her pencil flat under the first sentence, and started pulling it apart word by word. The verbs were brutal, the clauses stacked, but the nouns began to assemble into something. Grundwasser. Groundwater. Behörde. Authority. The first paragraph was not about the church or the committee at all. It was about water, and it was about the town.

"Payton," Mr. Chukwu said from his desk. "You're first."

The room's attention moved onto her like weather. She stood, her summary not written but half-guessed, held together by one paragraph she had decoded in six minutes and a structure she was betting her grade on. Behind her, Aicha gave a small nod that could have meant anything.

The article, she began in German, reports that the groundwater in the region is contaminated. She said it slowly, and the sentence held. The article says the authority found it in tests and told the residents not to drink the water. The opening paragraph carried the core story, the who and the what, and once she had said it aloud she understood why Arjun had underlined it twice: everything else in the piece leaned on it. The second paragraph, which she had skimmed, added that the contamination came from an old industrial site and that officials were investigating. The third paragraph, the one she had wasted nine minutes on, mentioned the church committee offering bottled water to families, and a resident complaining that the authorities were slow. It was true, what Arjun had said. The last paragraph was the part they could cut.

She sat down with ninety seconds of speaking behind her and her pulse loud in her ears. Mr. Chukwu made a note on his clipboard without expression, and Aicha leaned over.

"You were shaking," Aicha said.

"I was fine."

"You went last paragraph first, didn't you. I saw you." Aicha kept her voice low, her eyes on Arjun, who was standing now, clearing his throat for his turn. "He does this. He tells you the trick like he's being generous, and you spend your prep time feeling behind instead of reading."

Payton looked at Arjun at the front of the room, delivering his summary in an accent straighter than hers, the opening paragraph first, of course. It had not occurred to her until now that the trick and the timing might both be part of it, that helping her and rattling her could be the same gesture. She couldn't decide, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she couldn't, whether she was grateful or played.

Mr. Chukwu called for the next article, and Payton turned her paper over and read the headline properly for the first time. The town in the German article had a name she recognized after a second, because her mother had grown up thirty kilometers from it, and her grandmother still drew her water from a well. She looked at the clock, then at Aicha, and slid the paper across the table.

"Look at the first paragraph," Payton said. "Tell me if I read that right."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
Megan had taped her capacitor to the corner of the display table where the laminate was already peeling, and she kept one finger pressed on the tape while she read the folded note again. Isla had written it during lunch, in purple pen, before the bus: "You'll be fine. Judges love it when you admit what you don't know. Just don't expatiate on the history of the Leyden jar like you did in class. Ten minutes, Mr. Rahman said. Ten minutes." Megan folded the note small and put it in her blazer pocket, next to the multimeter leads.

The science museum had given them the atrium for the fair, between the pendulum and the wall of illuminated periodic tables. Sydnee's table was two down from hers, a model of a water treatment plant with dyed water cycling through gravel. Sydnee came over while the judges were still at the far end, chewing the end of a glow bracelet. "What's the field between your plates?" she asked. "Numerically. Mrs. Chen will ask."

"I don't know yet," Megan said. "I know the voltage. I set it to three hundred volts with the supply. And I measured the gap with calipers. Six millimetres, roughly." She looked at the two aluminium sheets facing each other across their air gap, humble and a little crooked, one of them still bearing the ghost of a price sticker.

"That's it, then," Sydnee said, already drifting back toward her gravel. "Ask Mr. Rahman if you don't believe me. He made us derive it in October."

Megan turned it over while a family with a stroller stopped at her table. Voltage divided by distance. Three hundred divided by six millimetres. She wrote it on the margin of her handout, in pencil so she could be wrong quietly, and worked the unit through: volts per metre, which, she realised with a small tightness in her chest, was the same thing as newtons per coulomb, the force on each bit of charge. She had been thinking of the field as a fog, a mood between the plates. It was a quotient. You could just divide.

The first judge was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, who looked at the display board for a long moment and then said, "Walk me through what's happening between the plates." Megan heard herself start on the history of capacitance, heard Isla's purple pen in her head, and stopped. "The electric field strength between two parallel plates," she said instead, "equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them. E equals V over d. Mine is three hundred volts over six millimetres, so fifty kilovolts per metre." She touched the gap with the caliper tip, careful not to bridge it. The judge nodded once and moved on to Sydnee's water.

Mr. Rahman arrived between judging rounds, holding a coffee he plainly wasn't allowed to have in the atrium. "Heard you used the ratio," he said. "Good. It's a heuristic in the best sense, a shortcut that happens to be exact, as long as the plates are parallel and the point is between them and away from the edges. Near the edges it fringes." He gestured vaguely with the coffee, as if the fringing were visible, and in the dim hall light Megan thought she could almost pretend it was. "What stays uncertain for you?" he asked, because that was always his question.

"Whether I actually understand it," Megan said, "or whether I just learned that dividing two numbers I have gives a third number I want. The field's invisible. I can't check it the way Sydnee can check her water. If my result were deleterious to my whole argument, some number that broke the display board, would I even notice, or would I trust it because it's clean?" Mr. Rahman considered this without hurrying, and a boy pressed his face to the glass nearby, watching the pendulum swing its slow erosion of the standing blocks.

He said, "Ask the judge if you can hang a charged foil strip in the gap. Watch which way it leans." Then Isla was at her elbow, breathless from the escalator, and the atrium lights dimmed for the planetarium show that ran every hour on the hour, and Megan picked up the foil strip with the insulated tweezers and held it at the gap between the plates.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
The museum was nearly empty by four o'clock, the light through the atrium glass going crepuscular and grey, and Nathaniel had the biochemistry hall more or less to himself except for Lilian, who was reading plaques at her usual pace, which was slow, and Noel, who was pretending he hadn't come for the biology at all. They had an exam on Tuesday. Cellular respiration, glucose to ATP, the whole winding staircase of it, and Nathaniel had failed the first attempt so thoroughly that Ms. Xu had offered the retake without a platitude attached, which somehow made it worse. "You can memorize the pathway," she'd said, "or you can understand it. Only one of those survives a hard question." He'd been chewing on that for a week.

He stopped in front of a model mounted in a glass case, half a metre tall, all bright plastic and chrome. A bent stalk, a knob, a ring of what looked like paddles, and a flywheel at the bottom. When he pressed the button on the case, the flywheel spun. That was all. No glucose, no flame, nothing he recognized from his diagrams, which were rectangles and arrows and had never once moved.

"Is that supposed to be a turbine?" Noel said over his shoulder. "Because it looks like a turbine."

"It's supposed to be an enzyme," Lilian said, and read aloud from the small card beside the button: "ATP synthase, the enzyme that builds ATP. Protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP." She frowned. "That can't be right. Enzymes don't spin."

Nathaniel pressed the button again and watched the flywheel turn, the little chrome dome at the top rotating against the stationary stalk. Somewhere in his notes there was a page titled THE ELECTRON TRANSPORT CHAIN, and beneath it a diagram of the inner mitochondrial membrane crowded with protein complexes, and a label he had copied without thinking: proton gradient. He had imputed meaning to that label at the time, assumed it was just another term to recite, another thing to pour into the exam and hope it stayed there. He hadn't once imagined movement.

"Wait," he said. "The protons pile up on one side. That's what the gradient is. And then they come back through." He touched the glass over the model's central stalk. "Through this."

"Through the enzyme," Lilian said, but she said it slowly, the way she said things when she was revising her own position in real time. "It's a channel and a motor at once. It lets the protons through, and the flow makes part of it turn."

"Like water through a mill wheel," Noel said, and then, defensive, "What? I've seen a mill. On holiday. It's the same idea."

Nathaniel had spent two years thinking of cells as chemistry, as equations balanced on both sides, static and dignified. The diagrams had let him believe that. Glycolysis was a line of arrows; the Krebs cycle was a circle; the mitochondrion was a bean-shaped oval with a squiggle inside. Nothing in any of it had suggested a rotary motor small enough to stand inside a cell, spinning ten thousand times a minute, though he did not know if that number was true and did not say it. He only knew the model was turning in front of him, and that somewhere in the diagram the arrows had been standing in for this, standing in for spinning, and he had never thought to ask what the arrows were doing.

"So the protons don't make ATP directly," he said, working it through with his hands on the case. "They make the spin. And the spin builds the ATP. The flow is the fuel, but the rotation is the machine doing the work." He heard himself and stopped, aware of Lilian watching him with an expression he couldn't read, and for a moment he assumed she was impatient, that she'd understood this weeks ago and was waiting for him to catch up. He was braced for the platitude, the "there you go," the pat closing.

"You failed the exam," she said instead, "and now you understand it better than I do."

He looked at her. "I don't understand it better. I understand this one piece."

"That's the piece I've been faking for a month," Lilian said. "I can recite the whole pathway. I couldn't have told you why anything moved." She pulled out her phone and photographed the model, the flywheel still coasting to a stop, the card with its one plain sentence. "Ms. Xu is going to ask why. She always asks why."

Noel leaned against the neighbouring case, arms folded, studying the ceiling. "So Tuesday, when she asks what the gradient is for, you tell her it's water going through the mill."

Nathaniel laughed, and then didn't, because something was assembling itself behind the laugh. The retake was not going to be the same questions, Ms. Xu had made that clear. She would ask the hard thing, the why, and his first attempt had failed precisely because he'd filled the pages with recitation and no understanding, arrows with no flywheel. He could study the whole staircase again the old way, or he could accept that the pathway only made sense as motion, as things pouring and turning and being pushed, which was harder to memorize and harder to forget.

"I'm going back to the mitochondrion exhibit," he said. "The cross-section one. I want to look at the inner membrane again and picture every complex in it doing something. Moving, or pumping, or spinning."

"An hour before close," Noel said. "You want to spend it looking at a bean with a squiggle."

"Come if you want," Nathaniel said, already walking, and Lilian fell in beside him, phone still in her hand, the photograph of the spinning model bright on the screen between them.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The kitchen at his grandfather's house smelled of WD-40 and burnt coffee, and Ryder sat at the table with his phone face down beside a jar of bolts, rehearsing sentences he had not yet dared to say. His grandfather was at the sink, washing a carburetor part that probably did not need washing, the way he did things when he wanted to stay in the room without intruding. On the phone, waiting, was Dayton.

The problem had been building all season. Dayton had missed practice twice that month and, more than that, he had stopped throwing to the cut on the fast break, which was the whole shape of their offense. Ryder was captain now, an accident of seniority rather than merit, and the coach had said something to him in the parking lot that he was still turning over: your team, your conversation. What Ryder wanted was simple and impossible. He wanted Dayton to change without being hurt, and he wanted to be the kind of person who could say hard things plainly, and he could not see how both were available at once.

He had tried writing it out. The first draft, scrawled in the margin of his physics notes, began "you always mess up the break," and he had stared at it for a long time, half an hour, noticing how the sentence was true and useless at once. It felt like a verdict. It had no shape a person could hold onto, no handle anywhere.

The night before, Marie-Eve had sent him a photograph of a page from a psychology book she was reading for her elective, a passage about relationships and how they fail. He had read it twice under his blanket, screen dim. The psychologist, a man named Gottman, distinguished a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character. The difference was not tone. It was the target. He lay in the dark hearing the two words side by side, complaint and criticism, and thought about every adult conversation he had ever overheard through the walls of this house, his grandfather and his late grandmother arguing about the flooded garden with an ease that had confused him as a child, since they never seemed to lose each other in it. Now he understood they had been aiming at things, not at each other.

"You've been out here forty minutes," his grandfather said, drying his hands. "Phone's not getting heavier."

"It's not the phone." Ryder turned it over anyway. "Dayton missed practice twice. And he's freezing me out on the cut. If I say it wrong, I lose him for the season. If I don't say it, we lose the games anyway and he never knows why."

His grandfather set the part on the counter, beside the jar of alluvial soil he had sifted from the creek flats, saving it, he claimed, for tomatoes, though he had said that for three springs. "When your grandmother told me I talked over her at dinner, she said, you interrupted me twice tonight. Not, you're a rude man. I could fix twice. I couldn't fix rude."

Ryder looked at him. "That's a complaint," he said slowly. "Not criticism. One's about a behavior, the other's about who you are."

"If you say so," his grandfather said, and went back to the sink, and Ryder understood that the man had never named it in his life, had simply done it, the way some people have elocution without ever studying speech.

He called. Dayton picked up on the fourth ring, voice wary, wind in the background, out walking his dog along the drainage ditch. Ryder's rehearsed opening dissolved and he said the truest specific thing he had. "You missed practice twice this month, and in the last three games you haven't thrown the cut pass once. I need you on the break. That's it. That's what I wanted to say."

There was a silence long enough that Ryder watched his grandfather's hands stop moving in the water. Then Dayton said, "Nobody passed it to me all fall, so I stopped expecting it." And then, quieter, "You do the same thing, you know. You always call the play for yourself." The word always landed with a small weight, and Ryder recognized its shape instantly, because he had spent half the night learning to name it. He did not defend himself. He said, "Okay. Tell me the games. Specifically."

They talked for twenty more minutes, the kitchen light going yellow, the dog barking twice at something in the ditch grass. By the end they had agreed on one thing for Thursday's practice, the cut pass, and nothing else, and Dayton had promised nothing and Ryder had demanded nothing, which felt less like a resolution than like ground that might hold weight.

Afterward he sat with the dead phone in his hand while his grandfather poured the saved creek soil into a paper cup and pressed a seed into it with his thumb, unhurried, as though the floodplain had been waiting all along for exactly this.

"You going to tell Marie-Eve?" his grandfather asked.

"Tell her what?" Ryder said, still looking at the cup. "It worked and it didn't."

His grandfather laughed once, low, and set the cup on the windowsill facing south.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The party had spilled onto the patio because the dining room could not hold everyone, and Amy's mortarboard kept trying to escape her head every time the screen door banged and sent a gust across the yard. She had worn it all evening as a joke, or mostly as a joke, and now she was chasing it across the concrete for the second time, one hand holding the elastic of her dress so she could run.

"Sit on it," called Ali from the picnic table, where he was guarding the last of the potato salad. "Or give it up. You look like a person fighting a bird."

"It's the worst hat ever designed," Amy said, pinning it under her arm. "Four corners, completely flat, nothing to grip your skull. Why would they make it this shape? It's like they wanted it to fly away."

Mr. Sokolov, who lived next door and had come over with a bottle of wine and his usual taciturn nod, was stacking his plate by the fence. He did not turn around, but he must have been listening, because he said, without any particular warmth, "Bricklayers."

Everyone looked at him. Amy waited for more and got nothing, which was how conversations with Mr. Sokolov generally went, so she turned to her phone with the cap still clamped under her arm and typed it in. The result came up fast, and she read it twice before she said it out loud.

"It's called a mortarboard because it looks like the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar," she announced. "It's not a hat. It's a tool. We've all been balancing a bricklayer's tray on our heads and wondering why it doesn't fit."

Ali laughed hard enough that he had to set down his fork. Emie, who had been quiet at the end of the table all evening, did not laugh. She was drawing a small hard line in the potato salad with her spoon, and Amy, who had known her since fourth grade, recognized the sign.

"Can I talk to you," Emie said. It was not a question. She stood and walked to the far corner of the patio, near the hydrangeas, and Amy followed, still holding the cap.

"You told Mr. Sokolov's daughter I said her essay was fake," Emie said. "Two months ago. She asked me about it at the fair on Saturday."

Amy's first instinct was to remonstrate, to list the exact words she had used and the exact words she hadn't, but she stopped herself, because underneath that impulse she knew the shape of what she had done. She had said, laughing, to a group of people, that it was convenient Emie's winning essay happened to be about Mr. Sokolov's neighborhood, the one he'd written a whole op-ed about. She had meant it as a joke about coincidence. It had traveled as an accusation of plagiarism, and Emie had spent the spring being slightly less herself around her, and Amy had told herself that was just senior year, just distance, just everything ending.

"I said it wrong," Amy said. "I said it stupidly. I never thought you copied anything, but I can see how it landed."

"Everyone in honors English heard some version of it." Emie's voice stayed level, which was worse than if it had cracked. "I want it fixed before we leave for college. Not a note. Out loud, to the people who heard it."

Amy looked back at the table, at the aunt refilling glasses, at Mr. Sokolov eating his potato salad alone and unhurried, at Ali now narrating something with both hands. Two months of thinking about Emie and doing nothing. A reparation that could not be mailed or texted, that had to be said standing up in front of people who would watch her say it.

"Tonight," Amy said. "Before everyone leaves. I'll do it tonight."

"If you wait until it's convenient, it won't happen."

"I know. That's why I'm saying tonight and not fall." Amy turned the cap over in her hands, ran her thumb along the flat crown of it, the board that was never meant to sit on a head in the first place. She thought about how a thing could be designed for one purpose and pressed into another and still carry its original shape through four hundred years of graduations, and how an afternoon's carelessness could do the same, travel under a different name and land somewhere she never aimed it.

She walked back to the table and climbed onto the bench so she was taller than everyone, and she held the mortarboard up like a small flat flag.

"Before the cake," she said, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "I need to say something about Emie's essay, and about what I said about it, and I need the people who heard me to hear this part too."

Emie stayed by the hydrangeas, watching, arms folded, not close enough to rescue her if it went badly. The wind came through again and Amy had to press the cap flat to her head with one hand while she spoke.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: One month of free rent on a twelve-month lease at 1,200 dollars a month lowers the effective monthly rent to 1,100 dollars.
story:
Stanley spread the two leases across the library table like a dealer showing a bad hand. "Mr. Pereira wants us to pick one and defend it tomorrow. Mine has a pool."

"Yours is forty minutes from campus," Yuna said, without looking up from her copy. "That's not a pool, that's a swamp with better marketing."

Anna pulled her chair in and flipped the pages toward her. The assignment had sounded easy when Mr. Pereira announced it in homeroom: compare two apartments, work out the true monthly cost with utilities, present the math. He had even offered his own leases from a building he almost moved into years ago, back when he was young and, in his words, "financially noxious," a phrase he refused to explain. Now, staring at the fine print, Anna understood why he had laughed when he handed them out.

"Okay, so," she said, tapping the first page. "This one's twelve hundred a month, but they're running a move-in special. One month free if you sign a twelve-month lease."

Stanley leaned over her shoulder. "Free month. Done. Pool and a free month. I win, we can all go home."

"That's not how free works," Yuna said.

"It's exactly how free works. Free is the entire concept of free."

Anna was already writing numbers in the margin of her notebook, the way she did during exams, small and orderly. She liked arithmetic fine, but she liked catching things more, and something about "free" was nagging at her the way a wrong note in a song does. Eleven payments, not twelve. Eleven twelves. She did it twice because the first answer seemed too tidy.

"Thirteen thousand two hundred over the whole year," she said. "Divided by twelve months, that's eleven hundred a month. The free month isn't a gift, it just lowers the real rent by a hundred."

Stanley's mouth opened and closed. "That feels like a trick."

"It's a special," Yuna said. "Specials are tricks with confetti on them."

"That is a deeply cynical thing to say about confetti."

Anna recalibrate-d in her chair, sitting up straighter, and pulled the second lease over. This one was eleven-fifty a month, no special, no pool, five minutes from the grocery store. Utilities listed separately: water covered, electric not, which the first building's ad glossed over entirely. She started a second column in her notebook, and the numbers began to tell two different stories that both claimed to be the same story.

"Hold on," Stanley said, pointing at her page. "The first one's actually cheaper then. Eleven hundred effective versus eleven fifty. The pool palace wins on math. I'm going to frame your notebook."

"Electric," Anna said. "The first place makes you pay electric, the second doesn't, and the second is smaller, so it probably costs less to heat. But I don't actually know what electric costs. That's the part I can't get from paper."

Yuna frowned at the pages. "So what do you tell Pereira tomorrow?"

Anna chewed the end of her pen, which she knew was a noxious habit, the cap tasted faintly of pencil shavings and regret, but it helped her think. "I tell him the move-in special drops the twelve-hundred place to eleven hundred effective, and that it still might not win once you add utilities, and that I'd want a year of electric bills before I signed anything. He said defending uncertainty counts as an answer if you show your work."

"Since when is not knowing an answer?"

"Since he told us his econ teacher once asked him to define stagflation and he said 'a bad economy that's also rude,' and got partial credit for honesty."

Stanley laughed so loudly the librarian looked up from the desk and gave them the look, the one that could recalibrate an entire room's volume. He lowered his voice to a whisper. "Partial credit. So if I write 'the pool is nice' at the bottom of your math, that's honesty too."

"That's decoration," Anna said. She copied the two columns onto a clean sheet, drew a box around the eleven hundred, and under it wrote a smaller box around everything she didn't know. The smaller box was bigger. She slid the paper across to Stanley.

"Fine," he said, studying it. "But when I'm rich because I picked the pool, you're paying for the pool floats."

"Deal," Anna said, and signed her name at the bottom of the page like it was a lease.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
story:
The poster hung in the art shed at Camp Wenaki, pinned above the supply cupboard where the turpentine lived, and for the first three days Nathaniel pretended it wasn't there because he didn't know what to say about it. It was Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas, and tomorrow he had to stand up in front of everyone and critique it.

"You could just describe what you see," Raven said, sliding a jar of cadmium red across the table toward him. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Ms. Campbell-Brown literally gave you the structure." Raven had finished her critique of a Goya etching that morning and was now insufferable in the quiet way of someone who is trying not to be insufferable. "You talk about the two women, the hearts, the veins, the storm. Done. Go swim."

Nathaniel looked at the poster again. On the left sat a Frida in a white European dress with a torn, bleeding heart; on the right, a Frida in the Tehuana costume, holding a small portrait of Diego Rivera at the end of a vein, like a locket fed by blood. The two women held hands in the middle, and above them churned an empty grey sky. He knew the words for all of it. What he didn't know was what he actually thought, and the difference between those two things felt like the whole problem.

Calvin dropped into the chair beside him with his tablet, already talking. "I found a 3D tour of the museum. The Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City. You can zoom in until you see the brushstrokes." Calvin had declared himself Nathaniel's research assistant without being asked, partly out of friendship and partly, Nathaniel suspected, because Calvin's own critique of a Vermeer had gone badly and he wanted to route his ambition through someone else's success. "I'll pull up articles. There's this one scholar who says the painting is about divorce, another who says it's about national identity, and one who says it's both at once."

"That's twelve opinions that aren't mine," Nathaniel said.

"Since when do you need your own?" Calvin said it lightly, but Nathaniel heard something else underneath, the voice of a boy who had learned that borrowing other people's certainty was safer than owning his own doubt. Last spring, in English class, Nathaniel had done exactly that: he'd built an essay out of three critics' views of Hamlet, stitched them together with transitions, and received an A minus with a single comment in the margin in Ms. Campbell-Brown's handwriting, because she taught both grades, because she was the one running this camp elective too. The comment read, "Whose thinking is this?" He had never answered her. He'd just folded the page into his binder and felt it there, a small weight, every time he opened the thing.

That was the real reason he'd signed up for the art elective, though he'd told his parents it was for the studio time. Now, on the second-to-last night of camp, the assignment had caught up with him: a formal critique, colour, composition, symbolism, spoken aloud to fourteen people.

He got up and crossed the shed to the poster. Up close the paper surface dissolved into printer dots, and he thought about how the thing itself was an oil painting, a big one. He'd read the gallery label text Calvin had found and it had stuck with him, an odd concrete fact in the middle of all the interpretation: the painting was large, nearly square, about 173 centimetres on each side. He held his arms out in front of the poster, imagining it, a canvas roughly as wide as he was tall, two seated self-portraits side by side filling that square.

He walked to the far end of the shed, past the drying racks where the younger campers' watercolour landscapes undulated in the fan's breeze, all those wobbly green horizons. From across the room the poster changed. The two figures stopped being details and became a composition: symmetrical, monumental, the joined hands at the centre like a hinge. The exposed hearts on both sides made a second, hidden pair, one bleeding and one intact. The empty sky took up the whole upper half, and its greyness wasn't absence, it was pressure. He thought: she made it nearly square and put both women side by side because the painting isn't about one Frida choosing the other. It's about them coexisting, and the canvas has to hold both equally or the whole claim collapses.

The screen door banged. Ms. Campbell-Brown stood in the doorway with a flashlight, on her evening rounds. She saw him standing at the back wall, arms folded, staring.

"Find something?" she asked.

"I think it's about scale," he said, and heard how clumsy it sounded. "I mean, she's this big, the painting's this big." He spread his hands. "Almost 173 centimetres each side. Two of her, sitting side by side, filling it. And I was thinking about the sky, how it's half the picture and it's empty, and the red of the hearts is the only warm colour that isn't part of a costume, so it reads as the truest thing in the room. And the torn dress on the European one, the lace is all white like the alluvial silt we studied in geology, like something deposited, spread flat." He stopped, aware he was talking too fast. "I don't know yet what the scissors mean. I keep circling that."

She let the silence sit for a moment, the flashlight beam aimed at the floor. "Do you have to know?"

"Isn't that the point of symbolism?"

"Sometimes the honest critique says what it can't resolve," she said, and then, before he could decide whether that was permission or another question, she added, "Lights out in ten. Calvin, put the tablet away."

Calvin had been watching from the table, half lit by the screen. Raven had come back from the lake and was wringing her hair out in the doorway, and she said, "Say the part about the hinge again tomorrow. The joined hands."

The next evening, fourteen campers sat on paint-spattered stools in the shed, and Nathaniel stood beside the poster. He talked about the near-square format and the two seated figures, about the vertical seam where their hands met, about the arterial red against ceremonial colour. He talked about the empty sky as a decision, not a background. When he reached the scissors in the left Frida's lap, he stopped.

"I've read four explanations of these," he said. "I don't believe any of them completely. I think she cut something and I think the painting refuses to tell us whether the cutting was violence or surgery, and I'm going to leave it there."

Raven was nodding before he finished the sentence. Calvin had his hand raised already, holding his tablet like an offering, and Nathaniel looked at him across the room and shook his head, once, gently.

"Not yet," he said. "Ask me after."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
story:
Maria's kitchen table had become a country of rectangles. She had drawn the same curve six times, a lazy parabola sagging between zero and four, and under it she had packed columns of different widths: eight rectangles, then sixteen, then thirty-two, each one too tall or too short where it touched the curve, each one wrong in a way she could see but not fix. The assignment from Ms. Kerr was due Monday, a short report on the history of a calculus idea, and Maria had chosen the rectangle method because it looked easy. It was not easy. It was a room with the lights on and something still moving in the corner.

Isaak came over at four with his backpack still on one shoulder and a bag of clementines. He dropped into the chair across from her and peeled one, filling the kitchen with that sharp sweet oil, while Maria pushed a drawing toward him.

"Say the rectangles get thinner forever," she said. "Where do they go?"

"Nowhere. They just get thin." He sectioned the peel into a little star. "The number they add up to is the thing."

"The area," Maria said. "The actual area. Under the actual curve." But she didn't like the word forever. It felt like a promise no one could keep, a doorway you walk toward and never through. Isaak, who trusted limits the way he trusted gravity, shrugged and ate his clementine and said the whole idea was old news anyway, some dead German, and she should just look it up and be done.

That was the report part, and it turned out to be the part that changed things. Ms. Kerr had said one source minimum, so after dinner Maria sat on her bed with her laptop balanced on a pillow and typed rectangle method integral who. The answer came back fast, and she read it twice because the first time it sounded like a mistake, like something too strange to have actually happened to mathematics.

"Jonas," she called, because Jonas had come by to return her physics notes and was downstairs talking to her mother about plutocracy, of all things, some argument about whether the school board counted as one. She heard her mother laughing at him. Maria came down holding the laptop and read aloud: "It says here the definition of the integral, the rectangle method, is called Riemann. Bernhard Riemann gave it in 1854."

"In the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer," Jonas said, reading over her shoulder, "at the University of Göttingen."

"So the whole thing," Maria said, "the thing that took me four hours and half a notebook, that was his job interview."

She stood there in the doorway holding the laptop, and something rearranged itself quietly, the way furniture moves in a dream. She had been thinking of the integral as a mountain that admitted only geniuses, some grandiose peak that ordinary people photographed from the parking lot. But Riemann had stood in a room in Göttingen, probably sweating in a coat, and offered this as his ticket in. Not a summit. A threshold. He had made rectangles thinner and thinner and thinner and said, essentially, I will stand on this. And the people with the power to say no had looked at it and acceded, and the name stuck, and a hundred and seventy years later a girl at a kitchen table could not make the rectangles behave and it did not mean she was small.

She went back upstairs. The desk lamp buzzed. She could smell her mother's soup from the kitchen and hear Jonas still going, something about school boards and money, and Isaak had texted her a photo of his dog. She ignored all of it and took out a clean sheet.

She drew the curve once more. Then she drew the rectangles at a width she chose, not because it was right but because it was hers, and computed the sum, and wrote the answer down, and next to it wrote what would happen if the widths kept shrinking. She could not follow them all the way. She could stand at the edge of the forever and see the shape of what waited there, a region closing in from above and below, and she put a small check mark beside it, honest about the gap between her check mark and certainty.

Monday she would turn in the report. It would say Riemann, 1854, Göttingen, and it would also say, in her own handwriting at the bottom, that she had tried it herself, and that the answer moved as she watched it, and that she thought that was the point.

Below her window the streetlight came on. She picked up the pencil and drew one more rectangle, thinner than the last.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Evan arrived at the mall twenty minutes early, which he decided was worse than arriving late, because now he had nothing to do but stand near the fountain and rehearse things he would not actually say. Desirae had suggested the mall herself, offhandedly, the way she suggested most things, as though the outcome were never in doubt. He had agreed before he could think about it. Stephan, when he heard, had offered exactly one piece of advice: don't take her to the horror maze in the west wing, because he had read something once about what fear does to your judgment. Evan had laughed and then, walking to the mall through a capricious November wind that kept switching directions, had thought about it the whole way.

They met at the food court, and for the first ten minutes it was fine, better than fine. She had a way of asking questions that made him forget to be nervous, and he made her laugh twice at things he had not planned as jokes. Then she spotted the mini bowling lane tucked between the arcade and the shuttered photo studio, eight short lanes with purple lights, and suggested they play a game. He said yes. His hands were steady when he picked up the ball, and that felt like evidence of something.

They tied the first game. Neither of them wanted to admit how seriously they were taking it, so they settled the matter with a single tiebreaker frame, which Desirae won by three pins after Evan's ball clipped the gutter. His heart was hammering, hard enough that he could feel it in his throat, and when she stood close to him to gloat, holding out her hand for a congratulatory slap, the feeling intensified into something he recognized and did not recognize at once.

"Want to do the maze?" she asked. "The horror one. I've heard it's terrible, which is the point."

He said okay, and in the dark of the maze, with the recorded screams and the actor in the rubber mask who lunged at them at the halfway mark, her hand found his arm and stayed there, and his heart went from racing to something beyond racing. When they came out into the fluorescent light of the corridor, he was certain, absolutely certain, that what he felt was her. It was so strong it seemed like consonance, everything aligned at once, the fear and the person and the pulse.

He texted Stephan from the bathroom, and Stephan called him back instead of texting, which was Stephan's way of taking up space. "That thing I said," Stephan said. "It's real. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby." Evan said that was the least romantic sentence ever spoken. Stephan said that was rather the point.

Back at the food court, with pretzels, Evan tried to run the experiment on himself. He let his pulse settle. He looked at Desirae across the table, at the way she tore her pretzel into pieces before eating any of it, at the small argument she was making about whether malls were dying or evolving, and he checked, carefully, like a man taking his own temperature. Something was still there. Less thunderous, quieter, but present. He could not tell whether it had been there before the maze or whether the maze had only made him look.

He owed her something, though. He had spent an hour cataloguing his own heart while she talked, and she deserved better than an audience of one absent auditor. So he told her, badly, about the tiebreaker and the maze and the thing Stephan had said, expecting her to be offended that he had been doing arithmetic on a feeling. She was quiet for a moment, tearing the last of her pretzel into progressively smaller pieces. "So which is it?" she said finally. "The maze or me?"

"I think it's you," he said. "But I only think that because the maze ended and it didn't." It was not a smooth answer. She looked at him the way she looked at the bowling score, as if recalculating it. He felt he should expiate the whole clinical approach somehow, buy her another pretzel, start over, but she was already standing, slinging her bag over her shoulder.

"Okay," she said. "Then let's go back in the maze once more, and this time I'll hold your hand from the start, and you can tell me after whether your heart is lying."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron by using the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity.
story:
The playground at dusk had the advantage of being free, and the disadvantage of being where Nyla wanted to practice handstands. Lea spread her physics notes across a picnic table anyway, weighting the pages with her phone and a jar of iced coffee, while Noa read problems aloud from the study sheet with the gravity of a courtroom clerk.

"Two parallel plates, separated by five millimetres, connected to a potential difference of three hundred volts. Find the field strength at a point between them." Noa looked up. "Also, why is there a point? Isn't it the same everywhere in there?"

"Uniform," Lea said. "Supposedly. E equals V over d." She wrote it, then stopped, pen hovering. "I can do the arithmetic. I don't know what I'm doing, though. That's the part nobody warns you about. You can commodify a formula, sell it to me on a study sheet for twelve dollars, and I still can't feel it."

Nyla dropped out of a handstand against the climbing wall and wandered over, shaking blood back into her feet. She had a folded brochure from the science museum, where she'd spent the afternoon failing to be impressed. "They had this replica thing," she said, flattening the paper on the table. "Brass, mostly. A little chamber with two horizontal plates, one above the other, and a hole to spray oil in. A whole room for it. Gift shop sold electron plushies, if you believe that."

Lea tilted the brochure toward the last of the light, which had gone a jaundiced yellow over the treeline. "What was it for?"

"Something about measuring the charge of the electron. The sign said a guy called Millikan did it there, sort of. He used the electric field between the two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still, against gravity. Then the drops just hung there, like the plate was a sky."

Lea looked at the diagram: two parallel lines, a droplet suspended between them, an arrow pointing down and an arrow pointing up. She looked at her own notes: two parallel lines, a point P suspended between them. Something turned over quietly in her head, the way a key does in a lock you had assumed was painted on.

"Gravity pulls the drop down with mg," she said slowly. "The field pushes it up. If it's still, if it just hangs, then the electric force equals the weight. The field is balancing the whole planet." She pulled the page toward her and began again from the top. "So when they ask me for the field at a point between two plates, they're asking how hard that invisible thing is pushing. Three hundred volts across five millimetres. That's sixty thousand volts per metre." She checked it twice, because checking twice was the whole of her religion lately.

"Sixty thousand," Noa repeated. "That sounds like a lot."

"It sounds like a number," Lea said. "But the oil drop didn't care about the number. It only cared that the push up equalled the pull down, and it hung there, not falling, in a little brass room, while a man measured the charge of the electron off its stillness. The smallest charge there is, weighed against a planet." She was aware she was talking too much, and also that she did not want to stop.

Nyla tapped the climbing structure, whose roof was a flat disc on four posts, a disc hovering over the rubber ground like a plate. "So that's your two plates. Roof and floor. Somewhere in between, the pushing and pulling cancel out."

"Electrically, not literally," Lea said, but she was already staring at the space under the roof, the empty volume where a point P would be, imagining a droplet of oil the size of a period at the end of a sentence, motionless, indifferent to the genealogy of equations that had put it there. Whether she would still understand any of this by Monday, under exam conditions, without brass replicas and dying light, she genuinely could not say. She underlined E = V/d and wrote beneath it, holds the drop still, and let that be the record.

"Next problem," Noa said.

"Two plates, four millimetres apart, one hundred and eighty volts."

Lea put her pen down on the paper, looked once more at the shadowed gap beneath the climbing roof, and started to write.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
Anna's father had been quiet through the soup, which meant he was composing something, and by the time her mother set down the roast he had it ready.

"Your cousin's trial is Tuesday," he said. "They moved it again."

"Didn't they move it because of the magistrate's surgery?" Anna asked, passing the potatoes the wrong way, so that they traveled the whole table twice before landing near her father.

"The magistrate," her mother said, "is the least of it. The point is that if Aiden had left the pub when I told him, none of this would have happened. If he had gotten the nine-fortteen bus like a responsible person, he would be here eating roast with us and not facing a judge."

This was the third dinner in a row built around the same foundation, and Anna, who had spent the afternoon arguing with Celine about whether hypotheticals could ever be checked, found herself less patient than usual. "You say that like it's one option," she said. "It's not. It's a sentence about a world that didn't happen."

Her father looked up. "It's common sense."

"It's a counterfactual conditional," Anna said. "I learned the word on Tuesday. It describes what would have been true if things had been different. Like, if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it. And the Sally sentence only works because Sally doesn't own a donkey. The if part is usually false. That's the whole point of the form."

Her mother's truculent expression suggested she suspected Anna of inventing words at the table. "So you're saying we can't regret anything."

"No. I'm saying we can't check it." Anna cut her roast more carefully than the task required. "You can't run the night again with one variable changed. If he'd left five minutes earlier, maybe he'd have caught the bus, or maybe the bus was late and he'd have stood at the stop for forty minutes and met the same idiot with the scooter. You get one run of the world. The conditional is a story about all the other runs."

Her father set down his fork. "The defense is going to argue exactly that. Reasonable doubt, alternate timelines, the streetlight was out, whatever. And the prosecution will say the facts are the facts."

"And they're both telling stories," Anna said, "about a night nobody can rerun." She heard herself and winced. "That sounded like a poster. Sorry. But it's true, and it's also true that some of those stories are better than others. Dad's story, that leaving earlier would have prevented everything, assumes the bus was the thing that mattered. Celine says you can't even begin to weigh that without asking what else the five minutes would have changed."

Her mother relented enough to smile. "Celine is now an authority on regret?"

"Celine missed a bus once and spent a week telling everyone what would have happened if she'd left five minutes earlier. Then Alannah pointed out that she could never check it, not once, not ever, and Celine got so angry she threw a bread roll. But then she calmed down and said the anger itself was data." Anna served herself more soup that had gone cold, because it was something to do with her hands. "That's the part I keep going back and forth on. The story can't be checked, so is it worthless, or is it the only way we think about anything? Every plan is a conditional. If I apply early, I'll hear by December. If I go to Dublin, I'll amortize the cost of moving across two years of cheaper rent. You can't check those either until you've already chosen."

Her father was quiet for a moment, and the quiet was different from his composing quiet. "So I shouldn't say it anymore. The thing about the bus."

"That's not what I said." Anna put her spoon down. "I don't actually know what I said. I think the honest version is: the sentence is useful, and the sentence is uncheckable, and I can't make those two facts cancel each other out. They just sit there together."

"You're going to argue like this in college," her mother said, "and your professors are going to either love you or fear you."

"Probably both," Anna said. "Alannah says I should write the essay about Aiden. The one that's due Monday. She says a counterfactual conditional is technically a world where Sally owns the donkey, and a whole essay could live there."

Her father pushed his plate half an inch toward the center of the table, the way he did when a meal had become something other than a meal. "Write whatever you want. But on Tuesday, when we're sitting in that courtroom, keep the philosophy in your bag."

"I'll try," Anna said. "But if Aiden gets off, I'm taking full credit."

Her mother reached for the gravy. "If Aiden gets off, I'm making trifle."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The screen door banged twice before Nathan got it to close, and the smell of his grandfather's house met him all at once: cedar from the closet, coffee gone bitter on the warmer, and the lemon polish his grandmother had used long after she stopped knowing what she was polishing. Alexandru and Rocco came in behind him carrying the pop and the chip bags, and his grandfather stood up from the recliner faster than Nathan had seen him stand in a year.

"Game seven," his grandfather said, as if announcing a court date. He was wearing the old sweater, the one with the frayed cuff, and he had already arranged the remote on the armrest beside his glasses.

They settled in. Rocco took the floor pillow, Alexandru claimed the corner of the couch, and Nathan sat where he always sat, on the rug with his back against his grandfather's chair. The pre-game show ran its montage. Somewhere in the kitchen, Nathan's mother was arguing pleasantly with an aunt about whether to order pizza or make the pierogi.

It was Alexandru who started it, at the first intermission, scrolling his phone. "There's a thing at Dev's," he said. "Everyone's going. Rocco, we could still catch the second period somewhere."

Rocco looked at the screen, then at Nathan, then at the old man pretending to read the standings. "We drove out here," Rocco said. "This was the plan."

"The plan was the game," Alexandru said. "The game is happening. It'll keep happening without us sitting in this exact living room."

Nathan's grandfather turned the volume down two notches, which was his way of saying he had heard everything. On the table beside him sat a glass of tea that had gone turbid and cold, the milk clouding at the bottom, and Nathan thought about getting him a fresh one and didn't move.

Alexandru leaned toward Nathan and lowered his voice, but not enough. "One period. We watch the second here, then we go, and if it's tied we see the end at Dev's. It's not like you're going to remember this particular intermission."

Nathan let himself cogitate on that for a second, honestly, because Alexandru wasn't wrong in the way he usually was. He would probably not remember this intermission. But he thought he might remember his grandfather's face in the third period, if it went to overtime, if the cup came back to this city for the first time since before any of them were born.

"Tell them the thing," his grandfather said suddenly. "Tell them what you told me last month. About the trophy."

"What thing?" Rocco asked.

Nathan felt the old familiar heat in his ears. "It's nothing. I looked some stuff up."

"He's being modest," his grandfather said. "I'm not."

"It's the oldest," Nathan said. "Of any of them. The Stanley Cup was donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, and it was first awarded in 1893. It's the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America. Older than the football one, older than the basketball one. It was a governor general just giving it away, and it just kept going."

Silence held for a second, except for the commentators murmuring about the power play.

"That's actually kind of great," Rocco said. "A hundred and thirty years, and the same object. Guys lifted that thing in knee socks."

"My whole point," Nathan said, surprising himself by having one, "is that you don't skip a game because the game is always happening. The cup is always being won by somebody. But it was in this room, tonight, with him, maybe once. Maybe this is the once."

Alexandru looked at his phone, then put it face down on the coffee table without answering, which was its own kind of answer. "Fine," he said. "But if it's a blowout after the second, I'm taking the car and you two can listen on the radio like it's 1953."

In the kitchen Nathan's mother called that the pizza was twenty minutes out, and the argument about the pierogi had apparently been settled by making both. His grandfather reached down and put his hand on Nathan's shoulder, briefly, the way he did, and Nathan got up at last and made the fresh tea, carrying it back before the second period started, the steam rising clean over the last of the turbid glass.

The game tightened. Rocco shouted at a disallowed goal until the aunt shushed him with a pierogi. Alexandru forgot about Dev's by the midpoint of the third and was on his knees by the ten-minute mark, and when the tying goal went in with four minutes left, Nathan's grandfather rose out of the recliner with both fists clenched above his head, and nobody in the room thought about anything else.

It went to overtime. The house went absolutely quiet except for the refrigerator humming in the kitchen and the skates hissing on the ice. Nathan sat with his back against the chair, feeling his grandfather's breathing above him, quick and shallow, and he understood that he had chosen the room and not the reason, and that he could not have said which mattered more, and that when the puck finally went in, the whole house detonated at once, his grandfather shouting, Alexandru and Rocco hugging on the floor, his mother in the doorway with flour still on her hands, and the cup, the old cup, ninety minutes from being won again for the hundred and somethingth time, glinting on the screen above them all.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Antoine had rented the skates before Mattea arrived, which he now understood to be a mistake, because it meant he was standing at the rink rail with nothing to do with his hands when she walked in. He had spent three days rehearsing the plan in his head: laps, then hot chocolate, then laps again. It had seemed like erudition of a practical kind, a program of real sophistication, and now it felt like a script he'd written for characters he hadn't met. Mattea waved, took the rental skates from the counter, and sat down on the bench beside him to lace them.

"You're Talha's friend," she said. "He said you were funny."

"He lied," Antoine said, and she laughed, which he decided to count as a good sign.

The first twenty minutes went the way he'd hoped. She was a better skater than he was, patient when he wobbled, and she told a story about her little brother putting a sandwich in the VCR that made him laugh harder than the story deserved, out of nerves.
