Then, coming around the far turn, he caught his edge and went down hard on his hip, and when he reached up, Mattea took his arm to pull him up. Her grip closed above his elbow, tight enough that it went past helping and into something else, and when he winced she didn't loosen it. She kept hold of it through the next lap, her fingers wrapped there like a bracelet he hadn't agreed to wear.

At the wall by the scoreboard he said, lightly, that she could let go now, and she did, and smiled at him, and for a while the evening righted itself. They drank the hot chocolate. She had strong opinions about which playlist the rink should be using. He was starting to think the date might actually be going well, and that the arm thing was nothing, a person who just hadn't learned her own strength, when Talha appeared at the rail in his sneakers, jacket zipped to his chin.

"Talha. What are you doing here?"

"Open skate night, same as you." Talha's eyes moved to Mattea's hand, which had found Antoine's arm again, thumb pressing into the same spot, and Antoine saw his friend see it. Talha was a phlegmatic person by nature, slow to alarm, which was why Antoine trusted his alarms. "Can I borrow you a second? Zamboni door, quick."

Mattea raised her eyebrows but released the arm.

At the far end, by the machine's rumbling bulk, Talha kept his voice low. "Dude. Did you see how she grabs you? That's the third time she's yanked that arm, and the first one wasn't helping you up. I'm not trying to wreck your date."

"She's strong. Some people are just, like, physical."

Talha looked at him for a long moment. "In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence," he said. "One in twelve. We learned it in health, and I keep thinking about how that's somebody in every friend group. I'm not saying she's that. I'm saying it isn't nothing, and you keep deciding it's nothing, so somebody has to say it isn't."

Antoine's first instinct was to defend her, and his second was to defend himself, the date, the three days of planning, the whole structure of the evening, and only after those two instincts had spent themselves did a quieter thought arrive: that he actually didn't know. He had spent the night reading every gesture for signs of whether she liked him, which meant he had been reading everything as being about him. The grip on his arm hadn't been about him. It might not have been about anything. It also might have been exactly the thing it looked like, and the fact that he liked her was not evidence either way.

"She didn't hurt me," he said.

"I know. I watched you not mention it."

He skated back to Mattea slowly, buying the seconds. There were two ideas in his head, and neither would lie down: one said that naming a small wrong thing could kill something good before it had the chance to be good, and the other said that the small wrong things were how you found out, that the first date was precisely when it cost the least to say something. He could not make them agree. He decided to act anyway, on the version of himself he'd rather be.

"Hey," he said, when he reached her. "Good date so far. One thing, though, and it's small. When you grab my arm, it's actually kind of hard. Like it leaves marks kind of hard. I'm not mad. I just want to be able to tell you stuff."

Mattea's face did something complicated, and then settled, and she looked down at her hot chocolate for a long moment. "Nobody's ever said anything before," she said. "People usually just go quiet."

"I'm not going quiet."

"I know." She turned her cup in her hands. "My last boyfriend went quiet for eight months and then just disappeared." She looked up, and Antoine understood that he had gotten one true thing out of her, and that it did not portend anything he could predict, good or bad. "Can we skate? I think better moving."

They pushed off from the wall together, side by side, no hands anywhere, and took the first turn under the blue lights, and Talha watched them go from the rail, his jacket still zipped to his chin.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Exegesis means drawing a text's meaning out of its words and context, while eisegesis means reading one's own ideas into it, a distinction used to judge interpretations of scripture.
story:
The folding chairs had all been claimed by the time Liam arrived at his grandmother's house, so he stood near the kitchen door with his phone in his pocket and his debate notes folded into thirds, the way a person carries something he means to need. The tournament draw had been posted that morning. Monday, fourth period, he would argue against a resolution he half believed: that the dietary laws in Leviticus no longer bind anyone living now. His partner, Walker, had texted him a string of exclamation points and then gone silent, which was Walker's way of leaving the work to someone else.

His uncle held court at the head of the table, a raconteur with two glasses of wine in him already, retelling the story of a road trip through Kentucky as though the family had not heard it at every gathering since Liam was nine. Liam waited for the pause that always followed the punchline, then said, to no one in particular, "Can I ask everybody something? For a school thing."

Antonin looked up from across the table. Antonin was not family, technically; he was Ms. Whitehead's nephew, dragged along because his parents were abroad, and he had spent the afternoon being polite to strangers, which had visibly exhausted him. He was also, Liam knew from three years of shared classes, the sharpest opponent in the school's debate club, and the resolution had his name beside it as the negative. He set down his fork.

"The rules in Leviticus," Liam said. "No shellfish, no pork. Half the cafeteria quotes them as a joke, and the other half quotes them to shame people. My side has to argue they're obsolete. I have to argue it by Monday."

Antonin's grandmother, Ms. Whitehead herself, a retired teacher whom the family had invited because her street was icy and her kettle was broken, folded her napkin with great care. "And which do you actually think?" she asked, in a voice that suggested she had asked this question of students for forty years and remembered every answer.

"I don't know yet," Liam said, which was true in a way he hadn't planned to admit out loud.

"Then you'll lose," Antonin said. "Judges can smell an unexamined position." He turned his chair slightly, angling toward Liam, and the rest of the table diminished into noise. "Look. Last year I watched a kid argue that the Sabbath command was really about work-life balance, because that's what he already believed before he opened the text. He found rest culture in Exodus the way people find their own faces in clouds. Ms. Whitehead called it eisegesis. Reading yourself into the verse instead of drawing the verse out."

"Exegesis is the other thing," Liam said slowly. "Pulling the meaning out of the words and the context. Eisegesis is pushing your meaning in."

Antonin nodded once, and something like approval crossed his face and was immediately withdrawn. "So don't tell me the laws are outdated because bacon tastes good. That's not an argument, that's appetite wearing a hedonistic costume and calling itself ethics. Show me what the text was for. Then show me what changed, if anything did."

The uncle launched into another story, this one about a shrimp boil in 1994, and Liam half listened while his notes went soft in his sweating hand. He thought of his grandmother, who had kept kosher until the year his grandfather died and then stopped, without explanation, as if the rules had been a promise made to one person only. He had never asked her why. She was sitting three feet away, piling her plate with the roast everyone else was eating, and the question he needed was whether the old rule had been about God or about belonging, whether a law could disenfranchise the very people it was meant to gather in.

"Grandma," he said, interrupting the shrimp story, which earned him a glare from the uncle. "When you stopped keeping kosher. Was it because you decided it didn't apply, or because it applied to a life that ended?"

She looked at him for a long moment. "That is a Monday question asked on a Sunday," she said. "Come by tomorrow and help me make the soup, and we'll see."

Antonin caught Liam's eye across the table and tipped his head toward the door, meaning: we should talk strategy, and meaning also, Liam suspected, several other things. The kitchen clock read a quarter past eight. Monday was coming, and so was the soup, and so was a question he had been carrying folded into thirds for two years without ever opening it. He pushed back his chair.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
story:
The gym hired Ryan three weeks after his seventeenth birthday, and his whole job so far had been paper. He restocked the waiver binder, checked that every signature had a date beside it, and explained the terms to newcomers who never read them. "You sign here, and here, initials there," he said, all day, sliding the clipboard across the counter. Behind him the wall rose forty feet, routes taped in colors, and above the noise of falling he could hear the rope catch each time with a sound like a door closing.

On Thursday a woman came in with her son, maybe twelve, and stood at the counter reading the waiver the whole way through, which nobody did. She put her finger under a line about releasing the gym from all claims arising from negligence. "So if something happens, we can't sue," she said.

"Basically, yeah," Ryan said. He had said this enough times to believe it.

"Even if they left a bolt loose on purpose?"

Ryan stopped with the pen halfway to her. "I don't actually know," he said. "Let me ask my manager."

Ms. Bondarenko was in the back office doing the schedule. She was fifty, blunt, kept a jar of licorice on her desk, and Ryan liked her because she never talked down to him. He repeated the woman's question. Ms. Bondarenko took a licorice twist and snapped it in half before she answered.

"Read the waiver again," she said. "It says negligence. It doesn't say gross negligence, and it doesn't say intentional misconduct, because if it did, it wouldn't be worth the paper. Courts won't enforce a waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it. That's the line. A waiver can cover ordinary negligence, careless stuff, the risk you accept when you climb. It cannot cover somebody deciding to hurt you or not caring at all whether you live."

"So she can sue," Ryan said.

"She can sue over that. She can't sue over ordinary negligence, or she can sue but she'll lose. Go tell her the truth, not the sales pitch."

Ryan went back and told the woman, plainly, what Ms. Bondarenko had said. She signed, and her son climbed for two hours and fell twice, laughing both times.

That night Ryan looked it up on his own, because he wanted to see it somewhere other than a licorice jar. He had always been like that; his mother called him an autodidact, half mocking, half proud, and he'd stopped correcting her pronunciation years ago. He found a law site with the plain sentence Ms. Bondarenko had given him, word for word, and then three paragraphs of cases he didn't finish. He thought about how the gym commodified risk, selling it by the hour, and how the waiver was the receipt. Something about that felt clean and something felt wrong, and he couldn't separate the two feelings.

On Friday Shaylee came in with Chanelle. They were both on the gymnastics team at school and had decided climbing was the cheaper sport. Shaylee filled out the waiver standing up, scrawling her signature in four seconds, and Chanelle copied her. Ryan watched them and heard himself say, "You know what you're signing?"

Shaylee shrugged. "It says we won't sue if we get hurt."

"That's not exactly what it says." He took the clipboard back and pointed. "It's saying you accept the ordinary risks, ordinary negligence, a loose hold, a bad landing. If somebody here was grossly negligent, if they just didn't care whether you got killed, or if somebody hurt you on purpose, a court wouldn't enforce the waiver even though you signed it. They're still responsible for that. Signing isn't the end of it."

Chanelle looked at her form like it had changed shape. "So what am I agreeing to, then?"

"You're agreeing that climbing is dangerous and you know it. You're not agreeing to let them get away with anything." He stamped the forms and filed them. "The signature covers what it covers. It doesn't cover everything, no matter what it sounds like."

They climbed. Shaylee made it to the top of the green route on her second try and hung there with one hand, shouting down to Chanelle that it was easier than the beam. Ryan belayed a birthday party of nine-year-olds and checked a harness twice at the mom's request, and thought about the ancillary clause at the bottom of the waiver, the one about photos, which let the gym put climbers on its social media. That one bothered him more than the liability part. He'd been meaning to ask Ms. Bondarenko whether they could make it opt-in.

At closing, Ms. Bondarenko counted the drawer while Ryan stacked the rental shoes. He told her what he'd said to Shaylee and Chanelle.

"Good," she said, without looking up. "Most gyms don't tell people that. Legally they don't have to."

"Do you think we should? Put it in writing by the desk?"

She finished the count, wrote a number on the deposit slip, and capped her pen. "Draft something," she said, and slid the notepad across the counter to him.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile's maximum height equals the square of its initial vertical velocity divided by twice g.
story:
The launcher at the back of the physics lab had a cracked spring, and for three days nobody could coax it above a sputter, but on Thursday it resuscitated itself mid-period with a bang that sent a steel ball arcing over the demonstration bench and into the fume hood. Ms. Rodríguez caught it on the second bounce, held it up like evidence, and announced that since the equipment had opinions, the class might as well have some too. The assignment went up on the board: calculate, before the end of the period, whether the launcher set at forty degrees could clear the fence outside the lab window, which stood two and a half metres high and belonged, inconveniently, to the neighbour whose prize dahlias had already survived one incident.

Maika spread her notebook and stared at the launch speed taped to the launcher's side, fourteen metres per second, and at the angle, and felt the familiar suspicion that the problem was hiding something. Erin, working beside her, had already filled half a page and looked triumphant. "Forty degrees," Erin said, tapping her calculator. "You just put fourteen in and go." Maika didn't answer, because Erin's method struck her as only half right, and she couldn't yet say which half. The ball that had flown across the room hadn't traveled in a single clean direction; it had gone sideways and up at the same time, and the launcher's speed had to be doing two jobs at once.

She drew the velocity as a slanted arrow and then, underneath it, two more arrows: one flat, one vertical. Alistair leaned over from the next station. "What are those, shadows?" "Sort of," Maika said. "The speed splits. The sideways part keeps doing its own thing while the up part fights gravity." She squared the sine of forty degrees, multiplied by fourteen, and got a vertical velocity she believed in. The horizontal part she set aside, because the fence's height, not its distance along the ground, was the question that could get them in trouble with the neighbour.

The maximum height, she reasoned, was where the vertical velocity ran out, where everything the upward part had earned got spent. She squared her vertical number and divided by twice g, using nine point eight for g as they'd been told, and wrote the result in her most careful handwriting: four point three metres. She checked it twice. Ignoring air resistance, which Ms. Rodríguez insisted they were entitled to ignore, the ball would rise four point three metres at its peak, and the fence stood two and a half. There was room to spare, more than half again the fence's height.

"We clear it," she told Erin, and Erin, who had divided by g only once and arrived at a number so large it would have put the ball through a third-floor window, crossed out her work without argument. Alistair asked the question that mattered. "But how far back from the fence do we set it? The peak isn't at the fence." That was the part Maika had to admit she hadn't solved. She knew how high the ball would climb but not yet where along its flight it reached that height, and the launcher's position in the grass would decide everything. Her answer was tenable for the height and silent on the distance, and she said so out loud, which felt strange, like handing in a half-finished sentence.

Ms. Rodríguez came by, looked at the two shadow arrows, and asked only, "Which one does gravity touch?" Maika pointed to the vertical arrow. "Then that's the one that answers your fence," Ms. Rodríguez said, and moved on before Maika could decide whether she'd been praised or merely tolerated. On the way out, the class was granted five minutes in the side yard with the recovered ball and a borrowed measuring tape. A fine grey deposition of chalk dust had settled along the window ledge from years of misfired erasers, and Maika rubbed it off the tape before measuring two metres from the fence, an entirely guessed margin she defended to no one.

Alistair fired the launcher. The ball rose the way the arrows had promised, hung for a heartbeat at a height that looked, to Maika's calibrated eye, very close to four and a third metres, and came down on the far side of the fence with a soft thud among the dahlias. It had cleared, though the peak had occurred somewhere past the fence rather than above it, which meant her margin of error had been real and lucky. She climbed the low wall, retrieved the ball, and stood there a moment looking at the flattened daisy stems from some earlier class, some earlier spring.

When she came back over the wall, Erin was holding the notebook open to the shadow arrows. "Show me the split again," Erin said. "I want to do the next one without crossing anything out." Maika sat down on the wall, took back the pen, and drew the slanted arrow first, then the two beneath it. "The height part is the vertical one squared, over twice g," she said. "That gets you the peak. For the distance, we're going to need the flat part, and I don't know that yet, so tomorrow we do it in the lab." Erin wrote it down and underlined it twice.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The hillside cemetery above the town smelled of wet pine and incense, and Alexis stood with a bucket and a ladle, watching her aunt pour water over the grey stone marker. It was her third day in Japan, her first funeral that was not really a funeral anymore, just a visit. Her grandfather had died in the spring, before Alexis had learned more than forty words of his language, before she had worked up the nerve to ask him the questions she now carried around like stones.

"Here," her cousin said, pressing a thin bundle of incense into her hand. "You light it, you place it, you put your hands together. You don't have to say anything."

Alexis did it, and her hands shook so badly that the smoke wandered sideways instead of rising straight. Behind her, her mother was talking to the stone in a low, quick voice, the way she talked on the phone to her sister, and Alexis understood almost none of it, which felt like a kind of theft, that her mother had a whole relationship in a language Alexis had let herself be shut out of.

"He liked you," her cousin said later, on the bus down toward the river. "He kept the postcard you sent. The one with the raccoon on it."

"That was two years ago. I sent it because Mom made me."

"I know. He still kept it." Her cousin looked out the window. "That was one of his idiosyncrasies. He kept everything people gave him. Receipts, ticket stubs. There's a drawer at the house you should see."

At the riverbank, the light was going amber, and families were arriving with paper lanterns, each one lettered with a name. Someone had explained it to Alexis that morning, not a teacher, just a neighbour with a folded map in her hand: during Obon, families light fires at the start to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end they float lanterns down the river to guide the spirits back. Back, the neighbour had said, the way you'd guide a guest to the door at the end of a long visit. Alexis had nodded, and privately she had thought it sounded like something you'd say to a child, and then she had stood at the kitchen window watching her aunt sweep a room that was already clean, and had stopped thinking that.

Their lantern was white with the grandfather's name brushed down its face in black. Alexis's mother held it while an uncle lit the candle inside, cupping the flame against the river wind with both palms, and Alexis noticed that her mother's shoulders were bare under her shawl and that the aunt, without a word, stepped sideways to stand where the wind broke against her own body first. Small help, offered like breathing. Alexis moved closer on her mother's other side and did the same, though she felt ridiculous, a girl pretending to be a wall.

"It's not a goodbye exactly," her cousin said, kneeling at the water's edge with the lantern. "More like showing him the way out so he can find his way in again next year."

"Which is it?" Alexis asked. "Sending him off or keeping him?"

Her cousin considered this, really considered it, the lantern balanced on her palms. "Both. That's allowed here."

They set the lantern on the water together, four hands easing it out past the rocks, and it caught the current and swung, steadied, and joined the thin scattered procession already drifting downstream, small fires multiplying in the dusk. Alexis watched until she couldn't tell which light was his, and found she didn't need to. There was something atavistic in it, she thought, some old pull older than any doctrine, the whole species leaning toward a river at sundown with a little fire in its hands. And there was something else, something her own, more deliberate: the understanding that you could hold two things at once. That the boundaries of a life didn't end where you stopped knowing a person; they were drawn wider, redrawn, delimited not by language or by years but by what you were willing to carry forward.

She turned to say something to her mother and found her already looking at the water, tears running without noise, and Alexis did not reach for a speech or a hug. She took her mother's cold hand and stood with her, the two of them watching the lights go, until the aunt said, "Come, it's cold," and put a coat over both their shoulders at once.

At the house that night, Alexis opened the drawer her cousin had told her about. The postcard was there, the raccoon faded almost to grey, tucked under a rubber band with a receipt from a station and a strip of photo-booth pictures of her mother at sixteen, laughing. Alexis slid the postcard out and turned it over, and in careful pencil, in English, her grandfather had copied out the words she'd written, letter by letter, like a man teaching himself to read a door he intended to open someday.

She put it in her pocket and went to find her mother.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: US employers must generally give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is needed to file a tax return.
story:
The accountant's office smelled of toner and old carpet, and Leah sat across the desk from a woman whose nameplate read Ms. Warsame, holding her mother's shoebox of receipts like it might bite. She had offered to come because her mother worked nights and because Leah was the one in the family who read forms twice. On the counter behind the desk, a space heater ticked, and through the window the parking lot sat torpid under wet snow, cars not moving, the whole afternoon slowed to a crawl.

"I need to file too," Leah said, before she could lose her nerve. "I had a summer job. Frosty's Cream Corner." She slid her last paystub across the desk, its columns of tiny numbers, and watched Ms. Warsame tilt it toward the lamp.

"Then you'll need your W-2. Employers have to send it by the end of January. It shows last year's wages and the taxes they withheld." Ms. Warsame said it the way she seemed to say everything, flat and quick, already reaching for something else.

Leah's stomach dropped. She had assumed the paystub was enough, that the thing she'd been carrying around since August was the whole record. "It's February," she said. "The ninth."

"So call them."

The shoebox, meanwhile, had to be dealt with. Ms. Warsame went through her mother's receipts one by one, and Leah helped, sorting the crumpled strips from the grocery store, the gas station, the pharmacy. At the bottom of each receipt a smaller number sat below the total, added on: sales tax, a few dollars every time, multiplied across a year of buying things. Leah had never once thought about it, and now she couldn't stop seeing it. It was on the restaurant receipt from her own birthday dinner, tucked in the box by mistake. Everyone paid it, every purchase, quietly, the way you metabolize a meal without ever tasting the parts of it that keep you going.

"There," Ms. Warsame said, pulling a folded paper from the box. It was Leah's mother's paystub from the hospital. Gross pay at the top, then a ladder of subtractions: federal income tax withheld, state, Social Security, Medicare. The net pay, at the bottom, was so much smaller than the top number that Leah felt a faint embarrassment, as if she'd been caught not knowing a room in her own house.

"Is that fair?" she asked. "She works nights and they take all that."

Ms. Warsame didn't look up. "Fair is a big word for a Wednesday." She set the paystub aside. "Some of it comes back. That's what we're doing here. Deductions, credits. The return."

Leah sat with that. At school Mariam had been arguing all January about taxes, loudly, at lunch, saying the whole thing was theft with extra steps, and Elijah had argued back that roads and schools didn't grow on trees, and Leah had listened to both of them and said nothing because she genuinely didn't know. She'd thought not knowing was the honest position. Now, holding her mother's paystub in an office that smelled like toner, she understood that there was a difference between withholding judgment and just never having looked. Mariam saw the money leaving. Elijah saw what it paid for. The paystub showed both at once, the taking and, somewhere downstream, the returning, and the truth of it felt like an isthmus between her friends' two islands: narrow, walkable, but real land all the same.

"I'm going to call the shop," she said, and Ms. Warsame pointed her toward the phone in the hallway without ceremony.

Frosty's Cream Corner rang four times before a teenage voice picked up, someone new, someone Leah didn't recognize. "My name's Leah, I scooped ice cream there last summer. I never got my W-2. Ms. Warsame says the employer has to send it by the end of January."

"Hold on, my manager's here." A muffled conference. Then a woman's voice, the manager herself, tired: "We mailed a stack of them out, hon. Some came back. Addresses change. What's yours?"

Leah gave it, and the manager read it back, and there it was: the unit number was missing. The mailroom at her building sorted everything into boxes downstairs, and anything without a number went back. Fourteen dollars an hour all summer, taxes withheld on every cheque, and the paper record of it had been bouncing back to an ice cream shop forty minutes away since the end of January.

"It'll go out again tomorrow," the manager said. "First thing."

Leah thanked her twice and hung up. In the doorway of the office, she watched Ms. Warsame enter numbers from the shoebox into the computer, unhurried, the screen casting blue light up onto her face. It was possible the return would bring her mother some money back. It was possible it wouldn't be much. Leah didn't know yet, and she found she could stand not knowing, as long as she was standing in the room where the answer was being built.

"Sit," Ms. Warsame said, not looking up. "You're here. You might as well learn where your mother's money goes." She slid a receipt across the desk and tapped the small number at the bottom. "Start with this one."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
The clock over the whiteboard read 3:42, and Tyson had drawn the mitochondrion three times now, each attempt more apologetic than the last. The after-school review session had thinned to four students, and Ms. Ramos moved between benches with her mug of cold coffee, pausing at his shoulder long enough to frown at his diagram. Glucose went in, he understood that much, and ATP came out, and somewhere in between the whole thing doubled back on itself in a loop he could not make behave on paper. He had drawn arrows pointing both directions, crossed them out, drawn them again.

"Yours looks like a plate of spaghetti," Kingsley said from the next bench. Kingsley wanted the regional science medal more than he wanted sleep, apparently, because he had stayed every Tuesday and Thursday for a month, his notes annotated in three colors of pen. He was already through the practice sheet, flipped face down, while Tyson was still on question two.

Tyson didn't answer. He was looking at the word printed in the textbook's margin, a word that had been sliding past him all week: Krebs. The Krebs cycle. It sat in the middle of the chapter like a nameplate on a door, and he had memorized it for the quiz without once wondering about it. Now he wondered. "Why does it have a guy's name on it?" he asked the room. "Like, who decided that?"

Rose-Marie, who was there only because her mother had remonstrated with her about the C plus until she agreed to attend, looked up. "Somebody found it, I guess. That's how it works in science. You find something, it gets your name." She said it without much interest, taping a loose page back into her binder.

"That's it? He just found it?" Tyson turned the textbook sideways, as if the diagram would make more sense rotated ninety degrees. It didn't, though he noticed something he hadn't before: the loop had eight stations, and the last one fed back into the first. It wasn't a path at all. It was a wheel.

Ms. Ramos, rinsing her mug at the sink, said nothing, which Tyson had learned was her way of saying look it up yourself. He did, on the battered tablet bolted to the side bench, typing with two fingers while Kingsley watched over his shoulder. Hans Krebs, and it turned out he hadn't worked alone. A man named William Johnson had described the cycle with him, in 1937, and Tyson read the line twice because the year seemed impossibly recent, more recent than his grandmother. Krebs had shared a Nobel Prize for it in 1953, Physiology or Medicine, and Tyson sat with that for a moment. A prize for a circle. For noticing that a cell runs on a wheel that turns and turns, grinding out a little energy each rotation.

"Johnson doesn't get his name on it," Kingsley said. "That's rough." There was something in his voice Tyson hadn't expected, something almost wounded, as if he were auditing the fairness of history itself.

"Maybe the name isn't the point," Rose-Marie said, surprising herself, maybe, because she stopped taping. "Maybe the point is that somebody had to be stubborn enough to stare at a bunch of reactions until they bent into a circle. I'd rather be the one who saw the circle." She was obdurate about it, arms folded, in no mood to hear that credit mattered more than discovery, and Tyson found he half agreed with her and half didn't. The naming felt unfair to Johnson; the seeing felt like the real achievement; he could not make those two convictions lie flat against each other, the way he couldn't make the arrows behave.

He pulled his diagram back toward him. Under duress from the clock, twenty minutes left before the janitor came through, he erased the crossing lines and drew the loop as a loop, glucose feeding in at the top, the wheel turning, tiny ATP molecules peeling off like sparks off a grinder. It was still wrong in places, he was sure. He didn't know yet how the cell decided when to speed the wheel up or slow it down, and Ms. Ramos had already refused to tell him whether his arrows at station four pointed the right way. But the shape of it was finally true on the page, a circle where he had been drawing a road.

Kingsley leaned over, tapped the loop with his pen. "You drew the wheel before you drew the prize," he said.

Tyson looked at it, then at the tablet still open to the two names, and started filling in the eighth station.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
story:
The coffee shop on Delancey had a policy, unspoken but enforced by the barista's glare, that anyone occupying a table had to keep buying things, so Vincent's second hot chocolate sat cooling in front of him while Audrey-Anne spread the pieces of her persuasive essay across the table like evidence at a crime scene. Cassie had claimed the armchair and was reading the whole mess upside down, occasionally making a small noise of pity.

"It's due tomorrow," Audrey-Anne said. "Ms. Mensah wrote one thing on the draft. One thing. 'Your evidence is fine. So why doesn't it persuade me?' And a question mark. A question mark, Vincent. Like she's genuinely asking."

The essay argued that the city should not have furloughed library workers last spring instead of cutting elsewhere. Audrey-Anne had numbers, dates, testimony from a worker who'd gone six weeks without pay, a quote from the city comptroller. It was, as advertised, fine. Vincent read it twice, furloughing his own hot chocolate to the edge of the table, and felt the same wrongness Ms. Mensah must have felt, a kind of friction between the facts and the point that he couldn't name.

"Here's the thing," he said finally. "If I believe everything in your essay, I still don't know why I should be angry. You've shown me the workers lost pay. You've shown me the city had other options. But you never say the thing that connects them."

"That's insane, that's obviously the thing, the connection is obvious."

"Is it? Your dad got furloughed too, right? From the plant?" Vincent had learned, over four years of friendship, that this was a subject to approach the way you'd approach a dog asleep on stairs. "You never say why losing pay for six weeks is a harm the city is responsible for, rather than just a bad thing that happened. There's a difference."

Cassie lowered her book. "Oh, this is that skeleton thing. Toulmin. I read about it at two in the morning when I was avoiding my chem lab." She was already pulling out her phone. "Stephen Toulmin, 1958, a book called The Uses of Argument. He said an argument's backbone has three parts. Claim, which is what you're arguing. Grounds, the data, your evidence. And the warrant, which is why the grounds support the claim. Your grounds are all there. You never wrote the warrant."

Audrey-Anne stared at her. "You knew this existed and watched me suffer for a week?"

"You suffered at your house. Technically I watched you text about suffering."

"Write it down," Vincent said. "Warrant. Why the grounds support the claim." He was reaching for the phrase because it fit the friction he'd felt, the missing bone. If the evidence was the body, the warrant was whatever held the body upright, and Audrey-Anne's essay had been lying flat on the table from the beginning.

She uncapped a pen, then stopped. "Okay but what's my warrant, though. If losing pay is bad, that's just... true. Do I have to prove water is wet?"

"You might have to prove the city caused it on purpose," Cassie said. "Hypothetically. Like, if the council knew the reserve fund could cover payroll and chose the furloughs anyway because it was easier politically, then your data about the reserve fund suddenly means something. But if they genuinely had no money, your whole essay is yelling at a rockslide."

"A rockslide," Audrey-Anne said, "has never once asked for a statement from the comptroller."

They worked backward through the essay the way you'd reread a text from someone you suspect is angry at you, looking for what wasn't said. Vincent found that he liked this, liked the feeling of the argument having anatomy. He also found, halfway through the third paragraph, that Audrey-Anne had buried a line about the furloughed workers losing their health insurance for those six weeks, and he made her circle it, because it was the strongest thing in four pages and she'd treated it like a footnote.

"See, this is the problem with you," she said, circling it anyway. "You pathologize every essay like it has a disease with a name. 'Ah yes, the missing warrant, very common in patients your age.'"

"It is common in patients your age. Ms. Mensah's whole margin comment is the diagnosis. She just didn't write the prescription."

Cassie checked the time and announced that her nascent plan to study for the chem lab she'd avoided had died at two in the morning and would not be resurrected tonight, so she was staying. Audrey-Anne started a new paragraph at the top of a napkin, crossed it out, started again on actual paper: not the claim, which she already had, but the reason the claim followed, the bridge she'd assumed everyone could see.

Vincent drank the cold hot chocolate anyway, because the barista was watching, and because it still counted as a good evening. He didn't know if her essay would persuade Ms. Mensah this time; the council's motives were still murky, and honesty meant saying so on the page, some version of if this, then that. But the napkin now read, in Audrey-Anne's handwriting, bridge goes here, and that seemed like something.

"Read me the sentence," Cassie said, feet up on the armchair.

Audrey-Anne cleared her throat. "'The council has argued the furloughs were unavoidable. If the reserve fund shows otherwise, then the choice was not necessity but convenience, and convenience is not a reason the library workers should have gone without pay.'"

She looked up. "Well?"

"Bring that hot chocolate lady another one," Cassie said. "We're going to be here a while."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Under the US Credit CARD Act of 2009, card statements must show how long it would take to pay off the balance by making only the minimum payment.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and lemon cleaner, and Dylan had counted the money in his pocket twice on the bus: one hundred and forty dollars, saved from four months of mowing Ms. Morningstar's hill of a lawn. The phone he wanted, the one with the camera Dev kept insisting would make his photos stop looking like evidence, cost three hundred and ninety-nine. Dev worked weekends behind the counter and had texted him about a deal that ended tonight.

"Zero percent for twelve months," Dev said, sliding a glossy brochure across the glass. "You'd pay like thirty-three a month. That's nothing."

Matheo, who had come along mostly for the air conditioning, leaned on the display case. "Nothing plus the part you're not hearing," he said. Matheo's mother worked at a credit union and he talked about money the way other guys talked about scouts for the hockey team, with statistics and grievance.

Dylan turned the brochure over. On the back, in gray type smaller than the ingredients on a cereal box, was a box labeled Payment Information, and inside it two lines. The first said something about minimum payment due. The second, which he had to hold under the display light to read, said that if he made only the minimum payment each month, it would take a number of years to pay off the balance. The number of years was large enough that he read it three times, certain the first two readings had been wrong.

"Wait," he said. "This is zero percent."

"Zero percent for twelve months," Matheo said. "Then it jumps. That's the whole business model. The interest is what makes borrowed money cost more over time. Same thing backwards is why my mom's savings grow without her doing anything. Interest cuts both ways, like a saw."

Dev glanced toward the manager's office, then lowered his voice. "He's not wrong. My first paycheck here, I bought a console on a card. First statement came and there was this little table on it. Said if I paid the minimum it'd take me years, like actual years, to clear it. I thought it was a typo."

"Why would they print that?" Dylan asked. "On their own statement. It's like a warning label."

"Because they have to," Dev said. "It's the Credit CARD Act. 2009. Card statements have to tell you how long it takes to pay off the balance if you only make the minimum payment. The law makes them show you the trap."

Dylan stood there holding the brochure and did the arithmetic he could do in his head. Thirty-three dollars a month for a year was three hundred and ninety-six, which was fine, which was almost exactly the price, except that the fine print said the promotion ended and after that the interest would apply to whatever was left, and whatever was left would then grow the way Matheo's mother's savings grew, only in the wrong direction. He had a system for the lawn money: forty dollars every two weeks, half of it already spoken for by his mother's putative contribution to the family phone plan, a contribution she had promised but not yet confirmed. He could believe the promise, or he could believe the fine print. One of those beliefs had a legal department behind it.

He thought about Ms. Morningstar, who had once told his English class that her father refused credit his whole life and died with a coffee can of cash under the floorboards, and how she'd said it not as praise but as a kind of grief, because the coffee can had never earned a cent while the house around it tripled in value. Refusing the card wasn't the same as being safe. That was the part Matheo never quite said out loud: interest didn't have a morality. It didn't care whether you were borrowing or saving; it only cared which side of it you were standing on. Dylan didn't like how much of his future seemed to depend on which side of an invisible line some number put him on, a feeling close to determinism, as if the whole thing were decided before he walked in. But that wasn't quite honest either, because the brochure was in his hand and not yet signed, and deciding was still something he could do.

"Does the store do layaway?" he asked. "Or can I put a deposit down and pay the rest over the summer?"

"We can do a hold for two weeks," Dev said. "Thirty bucks deposit, comes off the price."

"Then hold it," Dylan said. "And if I don't come back with the rest, keep the thirty."

Matheo clapped him on the shoulder. "Look at you. A man of the saw."

Dylan took the receipt and folded it into his pocket beside the hundred and forty dollars, feeling the paper against the bills. He texted his mother from the doorway: how sure was she about the phone plan money, really. Then he looked back inside, where Dev was already helping a woman in a blue coat who was reading the back of a brochure with the same squint Dylan had worn a minute ago, holding it up to the light and frowning, and Dylan stepped back in and stood quietly beside her until she glanced over.

story:
Nathaniel had claimed the sunporch of his grandmother's house as his writing office, which meant he sat at a wicker table with a legal pad, three sharpened pencils, and a plate of her ginger snaps advancing toward staleness beside him. The assignment from Ms. Navarro was due in nine days: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in his own life, staged in the school's black box theater. He had chosen the fight. The one from last spring, when his brother came home late and their mother stood in the kitchen doorway holding a dish towel and said nothing for a full minute. He had a draft, and the draft was terrible.

"You've written 'I am angry at you' seven times," said Jannat, who had biked over with a binder of revisions she called her destruction copy. She flipped a page. "Eight. Your mother character says, 'You have broken my trust.' Who talks like that?"

"People in bad plays," Walter said from the daybed, where he was lying with his shoes off because Nathaniel's grandmother had a rule about shoes and a plastic hippo by the door to enforce it spiritually. "Nobody in your house said that stuff. I was there, sort of. I heard about it at lunch."

Nathaniel defended himself for a while, the way you defend something you already know is dying. He argued that audiences needed clarity. Jannat pointed out that his mother, in real life, had never once named what she felt; she had folded the dish towel into a smaller and smaller square while his brother invented excuses about a study group that did not exist. Walter said the folding was the good part. Nathaniel ate a stale cookie rather than concede immediately.

That evening his grandmother found him still on the porch, cross-legged now, the legal pad bristling with arrows. He tried to forestall her sympathy by announcing he was fine, just stuck, but she brought tea anyway and sat down with the sound of a person settling in for the duration. He read her the scene aloud, doing both voices, and felt foolish doing his mother's voice in front of the woman who had raised her. When he finished, his grandmother said only, "She didn't say any of that to him."

"I know. But it's a play. You have to make things clear."

She sipped her tea and looked out at the yard, where the neighbor's penurious little dog was patrolling the fence line as though guarding a fortune it did not have. "When I met your grandfather, I told him I liked his hat."

Nathaniel waited. "And?"

"That was all. He understood it anyway. He kept the hat until it fell apart." She patted his knee and went in to watch her program, leaving him with the tea, the legal pad, and the strange feeling that she had handed him something important in a paper bag with no label.

The next morning he tried an experiment. He crossed out every line in which a character announced a feeling, then wrote the scene again using only what people would actually say. His mother folded the dish towel. His brother said the study group had run long. His mother asked whether the study group met at the diner on Route Nine, because she had driven past the diner on Route Nine at ten o'clock and seen his car in the lot, and the car had been rocking in a way unhelpful to the study hypothesis. Nobody in the scene said angry, hurt, scared, or love, and yet the page radiated all four. He read it and got a chill he decided not to examine too closely.

On Monday he showed it to Ms. Navarro after class, claiming modestly that he had discovered something. She read it, and he watched her face do a thing teachers do when they are pleased and trying not to slow down the student's own process. "You've found subtext," she said. "The meaning beneath what the characters actually say." He wrote it on his hand, because it seemed like a word worth keeping, like a fish too good to throw back.

"It's like my grandma and the hat," he told Jannat and Walter at rehearsal that afternoon, back on the sunporch, scripts spread across the wicker table. Walter had been cast as the brother because he could do guileless arrogance better than anyone in the sophomore class, a virtuoso of shrugging. Jannat was directing, which meant she said things like "Fold the towel slower, you're rushing your own grief," and Walter folded slower, and somehow the folding got funnier and sadder at once, which was the whole trick of it as far as Nathaniel could tell.

They ran the scene end to end, and at the moment when his mother asked about the diner on Route Nine, his grandmother appeared in the doorway with a plate of sandwiches, watched Walter's face collapse into a confession without a single naming word, and nodded once, like a judge at a diving meet.

"He kept the hat," she said, setting down the plate. "It's in the hall closet if you want it for the production."

Walter looked at Nathaniel. Nathaniel looked at the closet door.
